I?d have to say no for the following reasons:1) the garden is actually very small (you can wonder through it in 15-20 minutes).2) even though the trees are nice to look at (debatable given how some of the trees are shackled to metal frames), there are lots of signs imploring you to see the deeper meaning and philosophical undertones of the plants and stones, many of which didn?t really make a lot of sense.3) the owner will probably come to meet you at some point which seems superficially like a nice touch, but it did feel a bit mechanical - he would then get a phone call about some new guests coming into the park and suddenly have to dash off (probably to make sure they left a good TripAdvisor review)All in all, there?s a lot of great nature to see in Jeju, especially if you want to get away from the chaos and ponder the meaning of life, but why not climb up Mt Hallasan or do an Olle trail instead, and then go and spend your 12000 won on a present for yourself

This is an awesome place to go with street sights and photography in mind, with all the locals and tourist here collectively, lots of items to see, and nearby jungang underground market. Visiting both, seems to be the smart thing to do. Interesting place but of course it is still a market.
This is a very good park. You can see a lot of varieties of flowers, trees, and birds in this park. Also, you have a chance to see two-dimensional caves.
This is a traditional Korean market selling wide variety of items including food, souvenirs and live seafood. Good to try some street food here.

This is a perfect one-day trip from Jeju, I can imagine it gets packed in season, but on this midweek October day we were pretty much the only people on the Olle trail around the island. It's mostly really easy to follow, with a mixture of red and blue ribbons tied to trees and fences, plus distinctive arrows at junctions. The trail is about 11.5km but we also climbed to the highest point and took a detour to another beach, dawdled, stopped for photos and snacks and still got round in less than 5 hours. Just time for a peanut ice-cream and a snooze on the beach before taking the ferry back. A really relaxing, varied day, like a step back in time to a simpler way of life. Highly recommended/

This is a nice park with a lot of different flower and tree species. It's worth a visit and also a good opportunity to have a walk. You can climb on top of the hill to have a 360 degrees view (there is also a small cemetery there, not easy to find : take the most  peripheral path). Even in autumn it is colorful !

This is a big park where you get to sample the attractions seen in Jeju . We enjoyed visiting the folk museum, flower and bonsai garden, Jeju stone park as well as the place where they have big palm trees. Our time was limited so we didn't really stay here for long.

This is a beautiful volcanic crater well worth visiting. It doesn?t take too long to reach the top from the entrance (despite the sometimes steep stairs). The views are magnificent as you ascend, from the summit, as well as when you descend. Plus there are various volcanic rock formations that you can appreciate along the way, both ascending and descending (the two paths are different). The crater is full of trees and grass of a very unique shade of green (I?ve seen this shade of green only in the vegetation of other extinct volcanic craters such as the ones in Tanzania). There are platforms to sit on at the summit from where you can appreciate the view. After descending, make sure to visit the cove where you can meet the Haenyeo or the traditional fisher women of Jejudo. The way to the cove is clearly marked with signboards and it?s only a couple of staircases down to the beach. The Haenyeo put up a performance twice a day, which is very touristy but interesting nevertheless. You can buy all kinds of fresh seafood from them and ask them to prepare it for you to eat at the restaurant. But it?s mostly eaten raw / semi-raw with various sauces and the typical side dishes. The sea weed is particularly good, which you get as a side dish. There is unfortunately no English menu. If you don?t want to eat raw seafood, after picking your seafood portion at the entrance, take it to the counter inside the restaurant and ask that it be stir-fried (?pokkum? in Korean). Beware that even when it?s stir-fried, it?ll still be more on the raw side than the fried side. The black sand beach in the cove is also a treat. If you look closely and attentively, you?ll find all sorts of marine life among the rocks, in the pools and on the sides of the mini cliffs facing the beach.

This huge place has many shops and stalls selling household items, fish and seafood.   And there is also the food street selling all kinds of local food.   Just be careful and remember which gate/entrance you enter or else you may find yourself lost and spend time trying to find your way out.

This hike round trip, if stopping at the witseoreum shelter is about 5.8 miles round trip.  But a better way is to go up Eorimok trail (2.9 miles) and come back down via Yeongsil trail from Witseoreum Shelter (2.3 miles) Constant uphill to the top, good views of the mountains and the city below after halfway mark, and clean fresh air make this hike very worthwhile.  the hike up Eorimok trail consists alternating thick square studded steps, Boardwalk, and grave bedded large stones.    The first half is rather boring.  You hike up through the forest and have a recurring doubt about the trail you have chosen.  However, once you leave the trees, the view opens up and while it isn't majestic, it is a very pretty view to soak in during the remainder of the trail.    There is a lookout post that provides a sweeping view of the city below, and if there are low clouds you will be above it giving you an even more amazing view.   At the shelter you can use the restroom and buy cup noodle soup at around 11am and then start the descend down Yeongsil Trail.  This trail provides a view of the opposite side of the mountain and also has a lookout post that is rather awesome, especially when clouds are speeding past you.  Since we had friends drop us off at the Eorimok trail and pick us up at the Yeongsil trail, transportation wasn't a problem.  But at the Yeongsil trailhead we saw plenty of taxis waiting for business.

This high peak volcano is worth going for climbing... We went with my friend early march, the path was still snowyall the way!  Better to bring some equipement although it is possible to rent shoes at the convenient store down there.We were in march in a very low touristic season so it was quite nice to hike under the frozen pine trees with a beautiful blue sky. I think in high season on weekend, it could be crowdy! As it is a volcano, the walk is really sportive, meaning 6-10% continously during 2h. Get the first plane area, bring some candy bar or fruit, water of course, you will be enjoy this break on the roof of south Korea :=)

This Hallim Park is a big area with the palm tree, tulips, cherry blossom, etc.  They also have some cave and near to the sea.  They have Historical Story since 1971 if you see the website.  We need to have 2-3 hours i think to go arround.  When i visit here last week, we still can see the tulips.

This forest of nutmeg trees are easily accessible and very easy and nice to take a walk - 2 easy trails which are around 1 to 2.2 km long - all easy terrain, just some stretches of little gravel roads. We enjoyed an hour's walk in the sunset and loved it. While travelling there, keep looking out for the road which is flanked by giant nutmeg trees, said to be filming location for several Korean romantic drama.

This forest has a nutmeg tree that is over 826 years old.  We enjoyed walking on the paths that weave through the forest.  Beautiful trees, flowers and lovely singing birds.  We saw a snake and loved the fresh smelling air.  There is a small store selling drinks and snacks and a small coffee shop.  No gift shop.  The paths are well maintained and very easy to walk on.

This crater is unlike the others seen on the island because it didn't form much of a surrounding cone due to its quick explosion without spewing much lava around. It is the only such kind of volcano seen in Korea.Apart from the special crater, there are miscanthus (the purple reed) and eulalia in different seasons. Very leisure walk around.We spent an hour inside, including a nap under the tree on a wooden swing.

This bridge in Seogwipo harbour goes across to a small island which takes about 20 minutes to walk around.? It is a nice place to go at sunset, there are nice views and many birds in the trees.? Also nearby are the Cheoniyeon waterfalls, and a few shops and cafes.

This botanical garden is well arranged, it enables you to travel around the world through its flora. Pleasant warm ambience, pretty flowers, trees and plants, outside garden too. Great for sunny days - you can admire the view of Hallasan volcano.
They sell mostly food, fruit and fish. Some other stuff like clothing and typical market style stuff is available. Just right next to the underground shopping street if you want to buy stuff.

There were a lot carter in jeju island, one of them is sangamburi.We went there by rent a car, from our hotel around 1 hour. The place is calm and nature. With mountain view, savana and trees all around.If you like nature, this place is one of your choice. One of korean movie was made there.When we entered the place, there's a garden, walked inside there's line of trees, in the middle, there's savana.Going further, you will find mountain view.

There is only specialty on this street which is black pork. There are rows of restaurants selling the famous Jeju black pork. It is a 'Must Eat' in Jeju. There are two kinds of people in the world: those who like their beaches to be overrun with screaming, writhing masses of tourists, and those who think being happy is important. And sure, this could be just another one of those jaded reviews written by a bitter old troll who has no other outlet for his vitriol than to misinform random strangers on the Internet, but it's not. I'm here to vehemently disabuse anyone who is thinking of having a quiet day at Hyeopjae beach out of a sense of civic duty. Yes, the beach itself is a soft sand frame for spectacular sunsets punctuated by occasionally clear blue-green waters, but it's also a growing epicenter for the worst kind of overbooked tourism. Pros: The beach itself is broad, and the area in front of the main beach lends itself to a safe experience for attended children: there is a large, open region of sand at low tide and shallow water at high tide for kids to play in.  The view is nice, and the sunsets are extravagant. There is camping nearby with good tree cover, adequate facilities for showering, stores for trinkets and swimming paraphernalia, and places to buy food and drink. There is also a small but growing night life near the beach that has a distinctly island feel, far from the thumping of your standard Korean club scene. Cons: The swimming area is unbelievably small, so not only does everyone get to experience a sardine style of   swimming   in water that rarely goes past the hips of an adult, the water is also full of sand and debris due to the high person-per-square-meter ratio. Visibility underwater is often zero, so don't expect to see fish on a busy day - which is pretty much the entire high season. There is garbage everywhere, both in the water, and in large, reeking piles near the parking lot. The noise is unbelievable (just like the parking) and the local restaurants - with only one or two exceptions - cater to the lowest common denominator for quality.  Hyeopjae is being targeted by packaged family tours, and yet there is a laughably inadequate infrastructure in place to ensure a safe, organized experience for children. The beautiful volcanic rocks along the sides of the beach and in some parts of the water are playgrounds of minor and major injury. The often unattended children that race up and down the beach are in no way warned about or protected from these hazards. The forest of beach umbrellas tightly packed on the   main beach   is both uncomfortably crowded and poorly organized for parents to keep an eye on their kids, and for kids to find their parents when they get lost. The lifeguards are simultaneously overworked and overzealous. They are simply too busy whistling at people to keep them safe from the dangers of hip-deep water (a strange and annoying tradition amongst Jeju lifeguards) to effectively keep an eye out for people - especially children - who are may be in real trouble.Bottom Line: If you've never had the chance to explore Jeju, you won?t know just how bad Hyeopjae is. Moreover, as I said in the beginning, some people actually enjoy the mass market appeal of tourist traps, and I don't begrudge them their tastes. All I'm saying is Jeju has an embarrassment of better beaches with better food and better facilities. In fact, you only have to travel up or down the road for 15 minutes in either direction to find beautiful, secluded areas where you lavish on an empty beach and swim in truly pristine waters. Q.E.D.

The world's largest nutmeg forest can be found on Jeju Island, South Korea.  A beautiful, old growth forest with a gigantic nutmeg tree as the central attraction, this forest offers quiet beauty to stroll through in a relaxed and rejuvenating atmosphere. The smell of nutmeg is distinct immediately upon entering.  Parts of the forest have beautiful red crushed stone walking paths and other parts have very well maintained wooden pathways.  To do the whole forest takes about 60 minutes at a comfortable pace.  Picture opportunities abound, and you'll likely be able to see wedding couples posing for their formal pictures amidst the beauty of the forest surroundings.  A great break from the hustle-bustle of other attractions, this forest offers the opportunity to enjoy nature in a very unique way.

The whole way from the car park to the falls itself was scenic. At the start was a pond with mandarin ducks and a bridge. There were various representative statues of Jeju. All along the way is a river, you go to the falls on one side and you can return on the other side of the river. Staying in Seogwipo, I was advised to take bus 780, with the first bus leaving about 6:30am or 7am & getting to Seongpanak around 7:30 or 8am. I thought about taking a taxi to get there earlier, but I found later in the day it wasn't necessary. I believe it's the same bus from Jeju City.There's a small carpark at the entrance and a little store with a few drinks and snacks on sale. Apart from the lunch hut near the summit (which only offered noodles with hot water & bottles of cold water), this was the only place to buy anything. So carry some food and water with you, enough to last 4 hours or so.It's a fairly pleasant walk. Most of the time you will be walking on ground or planks of wood, and at times there will be nothing but big rocks, although most people were walking. I think I was the only person with hiking boots.Yes it can be very steep at times but is by no means difficult, nothing more than a series of steps. Just take lots of rest breaks and you'll be fine. It should take anywhere from 2.5 to 3 hours to reach the cut-off mark (see next paragraph) then another 1 hour to the top, so as long as you leave before 9am or 10am it should be alright.Coming down can take anywhere from 2.5 to 3.5 hours in total.I thought the cut-off point was strange, having a man in an office stopping people trying to reach the summit after 1pm, especially when the sun doesn't go down until about 7pm. I would've thought that was plenty of time to get up and back. That's just Korea and their over-sensitive rules...Not a lot of scenery along the way, but it's nice to enjoy being surrounded by trees for most of the way. For the most part it will be quiet, although some of the locals spoke loudly or even had their phones out playing music which I thought was weird.A lot of Koreans seem to be on a mission to get it done as quickly as possible, and they certainly have the stamina to do it, so keep in mind at times you may have to deal with people almost pushing you aside to get past.The view from the top is worth the hike. You'll be extremely lucky to see the bottom (climb Seongnam if you want a nice view), but you're here to see the crater lake, which is quite lovely to see when the cloud clears.

Sangumburi crater is a designated Natural Monument touted as the world's only flatland crater. The car park entrance showcases several large rocks from the crater such as the volcanic bomb and lava tree mold. During the eruption, molten rock flew from the volcano into the air and cooled into many exotic shapes. The area near the crater also contain several traditional Jeju graves - wide, trapezoidal stone walls surrounding the burial mounds. Visitors can walk around the extinct volcano crater rim, peer into it but cannot venture inside the crater pit covered with lush vegetation. The hills and Hallasan surrounding the crater is a picture of serenity and rustic greenery. Sangumburi is especially popular in autumn when the slopes are covered in Jeju?s famous Eulalia. Crowds and couples will be lining up for photos among the tall plume-like, silver grass swaying in the breeze. At a quiet spot, listen to the whispers of the eulalia dancing against the blue sky to add a pensive mood to the autumn romance.  Note: KRW6000 entry fee is quite expensive. Closes at 6 pm, except Nov-Feb closing at 5 pm.

Sanbangsan (?곕갑?? isn't a really big mountain but it has an interesting and distinguishable shape. It is about an hour west of Seogwipo by bus which stops conveniently right in front of the mountain.There is a nice temple at the base of the mountain called Sanbanggulsa (?곕갑援댁궗) with a huge golden Buddha a wonderful view of the town below and the ocean and an army of miniature mint-coloured Buddhas (I think). All make for great photos. Further up the mountain (you can climb up a long flight of stairs) is a small temple in a cave with an even better view of the town below. Worth visiting if you have made it this far. There is also an interesting story about a monk who hid in the cave during a violent time (can't exactly remember details). Down below south of the street in front of the mountain is a really really nice coastal walk with impressive cliffs that have been ocean and wind-swept into wonderful formations. This place is called   Yongmeori Coast   and also makes for great picture. (Worth knowing that the coast closes during heavy rain for safety reasons.)(Also of interest in the area to some is Hamel's Ship (a replica/museum of an old Dutch ship that landed on Jeju ages ago and the story of the Dutchman that was held captive in the island) and horseback riding (though it's only in a circle). Sammu Park is a destination not likely to appear on the typical package-tour’s itinerary for Jeju Island, but this downtown Sin-Jeju gem has some singularly unique features for the intrepid visitor.? First, the park was actually constructed on one of Jeju’s 368 oreums, local dialect for a small scoria (cinder) cone or parasitic/parallel volcano.? This one is Beduri oreum, surely one of the smaller ones, topping out at just 10 meters above its base with a circumference of 617 meters.? Beduri was transformed into the park in 1978 as part of an urban planning initiative. In addition to a large assortment of exercise equipment,? a children’s play area, badminton and basketball courts, and jogging/hiking trails, Beduri boasts a majestic, two-story octagonal pavilion, called Sammujeong. ? Constructed in the traditional Korean style and ringed by pine trees, the colorful wooden pavilion is almost like a giant tree-house.? It isn’t unusual to hear musicians and vocalists practicing there, taking advantage of the spot’s natural acoustics.? It’s a peaceful place to sip a beverage in any season.? Next, are you a train enthusiast or history buff?? Then you might want to visit Sammu for this feature alone:? the park is home to the last remaining steam locomotive for coal transportation in Korea.? MIKA Steam Locomotive No. 304 (registered Cultural Heritage No. 414) was manufactured in Japan in 1944, during Japanese colonial rule, and operated on Korean railroads until 1967. In 1978, President Park Chung Hee had it shipped to the park on Children’s Day, so that Jeju’s children could see a real train.? The train’s passenger car now contains a children’s library.? Finally, beginning in 2014, the park has been further renovated to be a sort of extension to the Bao Jian Street tourism and shopping district.? At the park’s south entrance, there is a giant clock surrounded by wildflowers and neon lampposts that match those on Bao Jian.? The clock has a Plexiglas dome that gives its neon face a trick-art, psychedelic look after dark.? Sammu Park is definitely worth a visit, particularly if you are staying at an area accommodation or if you will be going to Bao Jian…a chance for a little Jeju “nightlife.”

Our guide brought us to this place, let us alight and asked us to observe the strange phenomenon. He switched off the car engine and we saw the car still moving uphill without the engine switched on. He then demonstrated by pouring a bottle of water at one spot along the road and we could see the trail of water wriggled its way uphill without the application of any external interferences. The phenomenon was strange and unexplainable. Was it that a magnetic force beneath the earth on this road had triggered off that momentum? My guide did not explain and I could not find any explanation on any of the signboards around the vicinity. I remembered few years back when I was in Shanghai, I visited the mausoleum of the great Chinese revolutionary martyr, Song Qingling which was located at the western part of the city. Prior to her demise, she had requested that her body be buried at this cemetery site beside her late parents, the influential and rich Song family. I was astonished to learn from our tour guide and saw with my own eyes the strange phenomenon of the cypress and pine trees planted around the mausoleum was bending inwards and downwards from all angles towards the direction of the cemetery site where her body was buried. It was not just the left rows of trees, not just the right rows of trees but the trees planted at all the other corners surrounding the rectangular burial plot that were seen pointing inwards and downwards with the focus at the burial ground. The lush green trees appeared like bodyguards saluting, bending their heads and standing humbly for her directions. My guide informed us that the cemetery was a specially chosen grand and auspicious geomancy burial ground and that account for the strange phenomenon. The Chinese believed that if your body is buried on an auspiciously good Fengshui geomancy chosen ground, your future generations will benefit and prosper. I am not an expert in Fengshui and was hoping to get a scientific explanation for the weird phenomenon. Right here, at this strange mysterious road in Jeju, I was also trying to observe if the trees growing around the vicinity of the mysterious road bend towards and focused at the core center where the strange phenomenon occurred but I could not see what I saw at Song Qingling's mausoleum. Both strange phenomenon seemed to be unrelated in their nature and in terms of scientific theory of explanation that a strong magnetic force beneath the earth is in operation. The `Bermuda Triangle' is also another unexplainable phenomenon whereby it was unexplainable as to where so many ships vanished in strange occurring environment. I had watched a Chinese TV series on science whereby the film director sought to provide scientific explanations to the many strange `unexplainable' and `supernatural' phenomenon around China. I really hope that some days, the same film director could incorporate the strange phenomenon that occurred at this mysterious road, the ship vanishing Bermuda Triangle and that of the Song Qingling's burial site in his series and provide a scientific theoretical explanation for the weird occurrence. The visit to this mysterious road had triggered off my curiosity and I left the place, confused and thinking of the limits in science.

On Jeju Island's Halla Mountain--at 1,950 meters, South Korea's tallest-- can be found Korea’s highest paved roadway, known as 1100 Meter Road or the 1100 Highland Rest Area.? There, you can take a self-paced nature hike on an elevated wooden walkway through a “volcanic” wetland; with its many lava rocks, trees and wildflowers, this place has an otherworldly beauty that you and your camera will love.? You’ll likely see lots of ravens, magpies and maybe some roe deer (be sure to stay alert for them along the highway if you are driving). Across the road, there’s a colorful cafe and shop, offering local beverage favorites and snacks, as well as souvenirs.? (They carry a good selection of galot clothing, made locally using persimmon-dyed fabrics.)? From the cafe’s observation deck, enjoy a perfect view of some of Halla’s most famous landmarks, including Yeongsil Folding Screen Rocks and the 500 Generals Rocks.This area takes on a very different character with each season, and locals often drive up to see the magnificent ice formations that form on the trees and rocks in the winter and spring, when Halla’s higher-elevation trails may be closed to hikers.? But it’s also a good choice for visitors who have limited time to climb, even when the higher trails are open, because it is possible to experience these incredible scenes at the 1100 Meter Road area.Not only is this a beautiful area, these days the 1100 Meter Highland is part of the Jeju Biosphere Reserve, a UNESCO and World Natural Heritage Site.A couple of points:? this attraction is actually located on Highway 1139, which will also take you past Eorimok, Yeongshil and Mysterious Road. You can drive or take an intercity-bus from either the Jeju City (north) or Jungman Resort area (south) side.? If you take a taxi, you should make a roundtrip reservation, allowing 1-2 hours there.? It’s a good idea to take at least a light jacket, even on a summer day, and for late fall to late spring, have a heavier coat, gloves and even a hat.? And don’t forget your shades and skin protection; even in winter, the sunlight can be strong on Hallasan.

On entering through the entrance, one comes to the palm tree avenue. Different types of palm trees and cactuses greet you.  Next up is the wild grass and flowers garden. Felt relax walking along the path. Further ahead  are the Hyeopjae and Ssangyong caves. These 2 caves were formed by an eruption of Mt Halla many years ago. The temperature inside the caves is around 18 degrees celsius throughout the year so walking inside was cooling. Look out for the famed natural monuments, Pillar, Mother , the two dragons up on the roof, stalactites and stalagmites, and Dr. Jin and the fox girl.. Coming out to the cave,Jeju stones greet you gesturing Welcome . Next proceed to Jae-am folk village where one can see thatched  roof houses with stone walls. Do take a photo with the tall statue of Stone Grandfather, Dolharubang.  Next  will be the bird garden where you will see parrots, pheasants, ostriches and elegant peacocks walking around spreading their colourful stunning feathers. The following spot is Jae-am stone exhibit hall  where over 200 stones are displayed. We were amazed by the natural stone sculptures in the shape of  birds and waterfall. Walking on , following the signs, one comes to water garden where you can see 5 beautiful ponds, capped by the grand waterfall.. Finally you will reach the last section, subtropical botanic garden where  there are palm trees, foliage plants, herbs  alongside parrots, lizards, snakes and tortoises. After all the walking and photo taking, proceed to have lunch at Dolharubang restaurant  to try Jeju's traditional foods, like the delicious pork bulgogi. Or you can have freshly made seafood at Palm  Tree Restaurant. Or if you do not wish to lunch, you can enjoy fresh herb beverages at  Herb Cafe.

My wife and I ascended Mount Hallasan in April. While it was cool in the morning, we soon had to tie our sweatshirts around our waist. We weren't sweating as much but we're winded trekking 9.6 kms. While that distance may seem daunting, the Seonpanak trail was not too difficult, even for non-trekkers like us. There are steps and wooden walkways but in parts you have to tread carefully as it gets rocky. The difficulty level steadily increases as you move upwards. But if you take little breaks and keep proceeding, your effort will be rewarded with breath taking views from the peak. However, we were well above the cloud level and there were green and brown hills as far as the eye could see. A word of caution - there are no sources of water on the way up (although it says there's portable water at the half point) and no shops once you start the trek. So carry energy drinks and bars, at least 3-4 big bottles of water (per person) and Jeju oranges. You can get all this from the shop at the base, at the start of the trail.
