Bears sold in the teddy bear shop doesn't appears to be of good quality as they all have coarse fur. Still an interesting place to go if you are in the area (quite a few interesting sites in the area), but not worth a solo trip just to go to the museum.

Quite interesting! The village represent the korean traditional village in the past, there is different setting for each house, which is represent each job and social status in the past. If you are a korean drama fan, fyi, the famous 'jewel in the palace' was partly filmed here.Entrance fee : free

Pretty much everything in Jeju is available here. Within the city, easily accessible via car, taxi, bus. There's the traditional market, seafood market, fruits & veggies, night market (6pm onwards). However the zones seem kinda grey cos clothes shop can be next to fish shop, snack shop next to shoe shop, you get the picture. We bought some dried seafood, snacks, fruits. Then popped over to the underground mall. Good place for those wanting to shop and see everything in 1 spot.
Plenty to see here including traditional houses, a museum and plenty of... stones. Nothing special but a nice place to enjoy a walk.

Our visit to this village was an amazing experience! We learned a lot about the history Jeju, specifically their culture and traditions. Jeju is known for its black pig pork and we were given the chance to see one at the backyard of one the old house in the village. Plus our hosts were very entertaining and discuss to us the unique heritage of Jeju. The traditional role of husband and wife, music played, beliefs, practices and their livelihood. Moreover, we were lucky because the house we visited was the location of the famous Jewel in the Palace. We were amazed with their stone structures. We took photos in almost every corner of the village. Everything there was just amazingly beautiful. The old houses, tress, the souvenirs stores being in house in the traditional homes, the government offices, the pavement, etc, everything was mesmerizing. The people are very kind, approachable and welcoming.

Our stay in Jeju coincide with the operational day of one of the biggest and oldest traditional market in Jeju - Grandma Market which runs on days that end with 7th of the calendar month. There are lots of other smaller scale traditional markets which are opened on different days (e.g days ending on 5th, 2nd, etc...) thru out the island but we were told that this is the biggest.There is also an area which are designated for elderly ladies aged 65 and above whereby they are not charged any fees for selling there, hence, the name of Grandma Market.Lots of things can be found in the market, from plants, to snacks to clothings to housewares. We bought some fresh ginseng, chilly flakes and also fresh gingko from the market (after tasting some that were steamed and sold as snacks), The gingko there is different from those that we get in MY (most imported from China). Their is more creamy in texture and rounded as compared to ours.Overall, quite an interesting walk for an hour or two if you're looking to buy some of foodstuff.

Our package tour brought us to upscale shopping centers and attractions that carry local and international brands. One of these was the Chilseongro Shopping Street. Fortunately, I had bookmarked Dongmun Market on Kakao map and it was a short walk from there. I had no plans to buy branded clothes (nor any clothes for that matter) so I ditched Chilseongro and headed to Dongmun.The Dongmun Market is a wet market, a traditional market. Pretty much everything in Jeju is available here?clothes, tangerines, chocolates, seafood, household items, food. The prices here were a lot lower than the chocolate stores and souvenir centers that our tour group operator brought us to.At Dongmun, you can haggle, especially if you buy plenty. I decided to buy chocolates to bring back home to our office staff. Since there were plenty of stalls selling chocolates, I compared prices first. I ended up buying from an elderly lady who offered the lowest price. I got more than 60 boxes and she gave me lots of freebies. There are stalls that had different types of food. Some even had live seafood available and they will cook it for you. I was too full to try out the local food, but I did miss having photos taken.There were a handful of stalls that sold kitsch souvenir items like keychains and magnets. There were two large stalls that had numerous items on display; their prices were high though. I ended up buying from the other stalls whose main items being sold were something else and just happened to have magnets and keychains on the side. Nevertheless, the prices at the souvenir shops in Seongsan IIchubong were lower; I wished I had bought there instead.

Our guide brought us here to understand the striking cultural lifestyle of the local folks of Jeju.  The unique and exquisite architectural design of the `primitive'' huts and cottages of the natives was impressive. The pair of well carved and exotic Jeju deities statues that were made from volcanic lava stood spiritually on guard at the entrance. The sculptures matched harmoniously with the decorative Kimchi clay vases left unattended in the manicured lush green lawn compound displaying a special cultural taste that reminded me of the unique Hindu traditions on the island of Bali. I always think that it is the vibrancy and dynamism of the native folk culture that made certain attractions so special. The unique Alisan native lifestyle in Taiwan is just remarkably outstanding and different from that of the Maori in New Zealand and again, distinctively unique from the Dayaks longhouse traditions. It is thus a pleasure and a must thing to do to visit a folk village in Jeju to look at how the culture of the natives and how it is being preserved here.  We were introduced to a guide speaker who showed us the many agricultural tools used by the local natives but the real commercialized promotion began when we were `lured' into a room with seats and the speaker started marketing a type of drinks made from `Wuweiji' traditional herb that grew in abundance in Jeju and is believed to strengthen and invigorates the mind and body. It looks like another `tourist trap' and on the pretext of going to the toilet, I escaped the aggressiveness of the marketing talk. I wandered around the cottage compound admiring the foliage and the surrounding native architectural designs until my group of friends came out from the promotion. One of my group members was anxious to purchase the `elixir' drinks to enhance her youthfulness and she shared the drinks with the rest in the group.   I came out from the cottage and saw there were many similar cottages around the village and there were many sales talk going on in the other cottages. The admission to this folk village was free but I am not sure if my guide earned any commission from the purchase of the herbal bottled drinks by my friend.Except for the commercialized promotion, it is interesting to visit a folk village in Jeju.

Our FIRST meal in JEJU and we were just spoilt for choices. This is traditional market and we had so much fun walking in the market.The large boxes of tangerines greets you at the entrance and as you explore further, you see endless rows of fresh seafood. We randomly selected some food and they tasted delicious!

Other than just a seafood market, there are lots of seafood restaurants serving very fresh seafood. Do check them out.Lots of shops selling their Jeju hallabong chocolates and we found them to be cheapest here.Very interesting market to see traders selling traditional Korean food and side dishes.

One of the famous traditional market that sell variety of foods, ranging from seafoods, fruits, and souvenirs. Try the toppokki, many local people are visiting that shop. It's spicy but taste nice. You may want to try it.

One of Jeju's traditional market. If you visit Jeju Island and wants something to remember your trip or you want something authentic Jeju Island food, this is the place for you. Tangerines are popular here and are very delicious. The mandarin chocolate is also one of the best sellers here. Its a must try.

On entering through the entrance, one comes to the palm tree avenue. Different types of palm trees and cactuses greet you.  Next up is the wild grass and flowers garden. Felt relax walking along the path. Further ahead  are the Hyeopjae and Ssangyong caves. These 2 caves were formed by an eruption of Mt Halla many years ago. The temperature inside the caves is around 18 degrees celsius throughout the year so walking inside was cooling. Look out for the famed natural monuments, Pillar, Mother , the two dragons up on the roof, stalactites and stalagmites, and Dr. Jin and the fox girl.. Coming out to the cave,Jeju stones greet you gesturing Welcome . Next proceed to Jae-am folk village where one can see thatched  roof houses with stone walls. Do take a photo with the tall statue of Stone Grandfather, Dolharubang.  Next  will be the bird garden where you will see parrots, pheasants, ostriches and elegant peacocks walking around spreading their colourful stunning feathers. The following spot is Jae-am stone exhibit hall  where over 200 stones are displayed. We were amazed by the natural stone sculptures in the shape of  birds and waterfall. Walking on , following the signs, one comes to water garden where you can see 5 beautiful ponds, capped by the grand waterfall.. Finally you will reach the last section, subtropical botanic garden where  there are palm trees, foliage plants, herbs  alongside parrots, lizards, snakes and tortoises. After all the walking and photo taking, proceed to have lunch at Dolharubang restaurant  to try Jeju's traditional foods, like the delicious pork bulgogi. Or you can have freshly made seafood at Palm  Tree Restaurant. Or if you do not wish to lunch, you can enjoy fresh herb beverages at  Herb Cafe.

Of all the places we visited in Jeju via our taxi tour, this is what I would rank as #1 (see  http://www.visitkorea.or.kr/enu/SI/SI_EN_3_1_1_1.jsp?cid=1121529), with Sunrise Peak as #2.  This is a Buddhist temple set in a vast very pretty land.  Interesting Buddha statues ? very exotic particularly for those who have never been to a Buddhist temple.  Our taxi guide politely asked, I believe a caretaker, to see if we can actually go inside the temple.  We were allowed.  I?m not sure if it was early or this is not a traditional tourist place, since we only saw very few people (as compared to the other temple in Busan packed with too many people.)  Felt a little bit odd being a tourist spectator in a house of worship, but glad we did.  The landscaping and statutes in the area were very interesting.  So there's more to see other than the temple itself. I would recommend this place for sure.  Would go back again if have the chance.  Hopefully with less rain this time.  Free to visit.

My hotel was almost next to exit 1 of this mall so spent quite a bit of time here shopping for Korean cosmetics but otherwise it's just a regular shopping center, nothing special. Didn't try any of the restaurants down there, as I'd prefer to spend more time in the open air. But this mall serves as a great connection point to many other areas of interest within the city including the Mok provincial government historical site and Dongmun traditional market, with clearly marked signs at each exit.

My friends and I pirposely went to this theme park as we are fans of the Bae Yong Jun drama- The Legend, when we planned this trip, we asked the tour agency to include this on our itinerary. The facade was like a fortress from the Joseon dynasty except for the cars in the parking lot, the ticket booth and te posters saying this place was the location for the drama    The Legend   with a big picture of BYJ. We feel like we travelled back in time, the entrance is the main village with the bridge and man-made lake, the houses are surreal as you can see inside its like 3D not only the facade of the house then as you turn right you will see the village for common people , its more hanok styles, there is a market place with plastic meats, beefs but lloked real and the center of the village has a big traditional bar , it has second fllor where you can go up and see the view of the rest of the village, there were chairs and tables with some traditional glasses and wine bottles where you can do some photoshoots, there were tradional rickshaw downstairs, and a well with water, then there's a big gambling house with tables, some traditional games, with a big wheel with numbers you can bet on it, then a high ranking official house where you can go inside, there were furnitures, a fire place, there's living room, bed rooms and a TV where the drama is being shown, they really used this for the drama, thenat the center if the whole theme park was the big palace, as there were big gates leading to the palace with the whole field with cobbled stones, the palace is just so surral, you can enter it, you can see receiving rooms for the royalties, the emperor's chair, the rooms for the royalties with huge bed, books made of bamboo so it looked like window blinds, then there' s a roomfilled with hanboks where you can wear them and take pictures with it, there were mannequins of the characters in the drama, there's a dungeon too where they filmed the slaves or criminals being? punished, there were other rooms as well like the dining room with huge and long dining table, ere's a garden too with waterfalls, whoa! its really like the whole Joseon dynasty vibe! We took a lot of time taking pictures of the whole place with every nook and cranny of this place, its really a place for those who are fans of the drama or BYJ or even if you are curious how they live during those times, its like we time travelled back to those kings, emperors, slaves, scholars. the entrance fee to the park is USD10 and you can stay as long as you like. We used a private car courtesy of our tour guide but its quite far from the city as I remember we travelled for at least an hour from our hotel Shilla,but its worth it.

Museum itself was not very impressive. The movie and display apparently critisized Japanese people for what they did in the past, which was not very pleasant thing to see. The neighborhood was quite interesting with many traditional houses remaining.

many themes in the park such as tulip garden, Canola, rapeseed, cherry blossom, more than 100 years old bonsai, folk village with traditional restaurant 竊fresh grilled mackerel竊, well decorated water pond, peacock and bird park and many more. The folk village still maintain the culture of living that one should not miss. One need half a day in completing visiting the park.

Many people go to travel in order to beautiful viewpoints(something new, special). In contrast, I prefer love to see more local traditional viewpoints. For example, Dongmun Market, this was traditional market in Jeju which could totally represent the ancient Jeju resident's market. I still remembered that because of Jeju's transportation wasn't simply because the notice language almost was Korean. Therefore, I and my friend was suffer for this situation in order to find the Dongmun Market. But no matter how we hurt for take wrong bus in long times, when we actually corrected to get off the bus to the Dongmun Market, we were very shocked, It was because that we can't find the entrance. Fortunately, we finally found that and surprised, amazed for it. Because Dongmun Market was very clear, we thought that the traditional market must dirty, but actually it was very clean. In my view, if you want to travel Jeju, I think join the tour group is the best way in order not to get lost.

Manjanggul is a must see when in Jeju. It is easy to get (near) there from the main bus terminal in Jeju City, just take bus 701. It drops at the highway at the crossroad (there is an audible announcement in English on the bus as well as written on the screen) in about an hour's time, or just under. From there you can walk (under two KM) or take a cab (about 1000 Won per person). There is also a large parking lot if you have your own car or take a taxi.The entrance fee is 2000 Won and once you have your entrance ticket you follow the crowds of people down the steep set of stairs (be careful - it can be a bit slippery) and into the cave itself. The floor of the lava tube can be difficult for some (elderly, disabled, children) as it is rather uneven and tends to be rather wet. With proper shoes one should be able to navigate the 1 kilometer tube with no issues. It isn't very lighted inside so take care and watch your step.It's a pretty cool (in every sense of the word) experience and definitely looks very different from a   normal cave   in that it is one long tube with high ceilings and lacking the traditional stalagmites/stalactites.if you have a tendency to get chilly, do take a sweater or light jacket as the temperature inside is cooler than the outside, regardless of the time of year.

Loved this place for its wide variety of food stuff and lunch dinner options. Their jeju chocolates, choco crunch etc are sold in packs of 6 or 10 and one of the better deals u can get as compared to other areas in Jeju. Whether it is to take in the sights of the variety of food sold in a traditional market, get some souvenirs for the folks at home or to grab a reasonable price meal, dongmun market has it all.

LEE Joong Seop Street is lovely and there are some art shops where you can do window shopping. Then this small street lead you to the house where Lee's family lived for certain period, in a 4.6m2 room for 4 family member. You will be stunned to see how small it is!! But they loved this place where they could hug all the time, kids, and the couple. Behind those free zone, the art museum is located. Admission is 1,500 KRW(1.10 USD, 0.80 Euro). You can request docent on the spot. Korean is always ready, for English, better to call in advance when you will visit. At the end of the street, there is small traditional market where you can get some street food and fresh fruits. Strongly recommend to visit to feel the artist' spirits who lived miserable period. He made lots of work for 6 years before he died, age of 40's. It looks like Van Gogh did lots of works during short period. Good to visit 3rd floor to enjoy the view toward south part of Ocean.

Jeju stone park was rated A by Korea Ministry of Culture and Tourism, in recognition that this park is excellent in term of its specialization in the theme of stone, differentiation from other facilities, and characteristics relating to mythology and the life of the people in the region.Get the map at the entrance and follow guided park course. Don't miss out the Jeju stone museum to know how the formation of Jeju Island. After a short nice walk from the entrance,the museum is just located in the basement of a building opposite the Sky Pond. Follow the map to look for Jeju traditional village with thatched roof houses. Before at the end of course, drop by the unique Gallery in the park which you may find artworks of domestic and foreign artists.It is indeed best travel Korea during Autum because even though it was sunny day, but the breeze was so cooling and the air was very refreshing. It is a museum as well as an ecological park. It is a very remarkable cultural park which sublimating nature in art ,really very fantastic.

Jeju is a volcanic island and the black lava that erupted from Mount Hallasan few thousands years ago are found almost every where. When we visited this attraction at Yongdam which is about 20 minutes drive from the Jeju airport, we could see the sea rocks and soils were black in color. The Yongdam rock was probably a volcanic rock that erupted and eroded down Mount Hallasan and over the years sculptured by natural forces of strong wind and rain and powerful sea waves into a structure of a `dragon head' . But the invisible hands of nature did not leave a distinctively well carved aesthetic product that deserved our admiration and appreciation. I really could not figure out the `dragon head' from the rock until my guide pointed out it to me. But black dragon in traditional Chinese folklore was supposed to symbolize bravery and auspicious luck and good fortunes to the people and visiting this attraction assumingly bring good luck and prosperity.Nevertheless, Jeju is exceptionally natural beauty and boasts of so many awesome and stunning natural scenic attractions which are so fascinating so lovely so magnificent that make me wondered if this was paradise on Earth. The air is fresh and you hardly find heavy machineries and factories with thick polluted smoke emitting out from the chimneys or the methane smell of diesel and petrol from vehicular emissions that is so typical in crowded cities. Jeju impressed me what nature is all about. From Yongmeori seashore, manjanggul caves, cheongjiyeon waterfalls to Hallasan National Park and Oedolgae Cliffs and this Yongdu-am dragon head rock, the physical geographical lessons appear no ending and I found intense pleasure in enjoying nature's silent whispers.

Jeju Hallim Park is a field of frontier spirit of a man who transformed a wasteland to a green paradise. Consisting nine different theme gardens and seasonal festivals, Hallim park is an international tourist attraction of Jeju island, South Korea exhibiting global species of plants and animals. It is 80 acre big and has nearly 1.2 million visitors every year. Visitor can also enjoy Jeju's traditional cuisine in our restaurants. (Gardens) 1. Subtropical botanic garden 2. Palm tree avenue 3. Wild grass and flower garden 4. Hyeopjae and Ssangyong cave 5. Jeju stone and bonsai garden 6. Jae-am folk village 7. Bird garden 8. Jeju stone exhibit hall 9. Water garden (Seasonal Festivals) Jan. - Daffodil Feb. - Ume flower Mar. - Tulip Apr. - Cherry blossoms May - Wild flower Jun. - Hydrangea Jul. thru Sep. - Water lily and lotus Oct. - Pumpkin Nov. - Chrysanthemum Dec. - Camelia (Restaurants and Cafe) - Palm tree restaurant - Dolharubang restaurant - Herb cafe

It's one of the biggest traditional markets and has many shops so you can buy almost anything you need.I usually go for seafood and vegetables which are fresh and low cost.  I particularly like raw fish (Sashimi) which can be purchased by fish (shop will catch a live one and cut sashimi while you watch) or pre-packaged (around $10 ~ 20)The market also has many street food, like spicy rice cake and pancake like dessert.It's not as clean/convenient as a shopping mall but has a lower price and more cultural feeling.

It's just a stadium with some architectural appeal but the shape tells a story  which is interesting. Try telling any football aficionado that it just a stadium and you will get howls of protest!From the 2002 FIFA World Cup it is designed around   the mouth of a volcano    and its roof in the shape of nets of traditional fishing boats in Jeju.So looking at it in that respect makes it more interesting.It was not open when we visited as of course there are no games here at the moment (although open during the summer months) so it was like looking into a fish bowl without the fish.Outside the stadium are many stone crafted 'dol hareubangs ' carved from porous basalt (volcanic rock).The statues' faces feature grinning expressions and bulging eyes without pupils  a long  broad nose  and slight smile and their hands rest on their bellies.These are quite common throughout Jeju and can be quite comic and a little suggestive!Have a peek here if in the area just to have at look at the stadium design and also the rock statues.Enjoy your visit!

It's a traditional market where you can shop for clothes, food and make up here. There's a few souvenir shop also. The price of the make up here at jeju is very cheap compared to the price in my country. It's like 1/4 price. If you wanna buy some clothes you have to bargain it. I visited it twice coz it's easy to reach with the jeju bus. Just stop at the dongmun market stop en then go down to tge basement.

It's a new experience to us. It's great. Just walk inside the maze until you find the way. Maybe try and get help from your friends who have reached the tower. It's a great activity. Got some traditional games to play as well. There are lots of big fat cats at the ticketing counter. So cute, so fluffy.

It;s amazing that in a modern country like South Korea, this traditional village is still well appreciated by the government either by Korean people. This village can describe the situation of the ancient life of Korean people. Now, the village people have to accept modern life and for survival they promote and sell a kind of traditional medicine made of the extract of horse meat.

It was a good place to  go and very interesting!people is friendly over there and they are glad to help youwith your tour, ohhh but they want to sell some traditional very expensive products, I didn't buy but they still nice.
It is traditional market in the morning. Can buy many local products here. During night time, there are many food stalls open n more crowded.

It is one of the few villages that still exist on Jeju with complete retention of the traditional houses. The villagers still live in these houses but with modernized technology. They no longer uses the open air toilets, rearing black pigs and using electricity for lights, television and wifi. This is also the village that Dae Chang Guem were filmed in the early 2000s. Interesting to walk in the village as if we have travelled the time back in the past.

It is an attraction for people to take photos of the special ?Dragon? like stone with the endless sea. That stone is 100% organic and experience years of erosions to form today?s ?Dragon? appearance. You can spend a couple of minutes with that ?Dragon? and spend another few minutes buying and enjoying the traditional outdoor cuisines. If you are interested in buying souvenirs like key chains or the ?Dragon? like badges, there is a shop for you to go shopping. Even though the viewpoint just for people to take a photo, there would always be many tourists standing in front of the best position for taking photos, so if there are many tour groups at the moment, you really have to spend time on waiting for just a photo. So, if you don?t mind the feel of crowded or if you get plenty of time, you are recommended as it is a special attraction in Jeju. It is nearby the international airport of Jeju so you can go there at the time you arrived or before you leave Jeju.

Interesting guided tour of a traditional Jeju village, showing how people in Jeju used to live. Tour was conducted in mandarin, as we were a group from Singapore. Interesting highlights include the different meanings of the poles (at the front door), the outhouse (with a pig in it) and their honeyed drink (with some kind of berry in it).  They did bring us into a small room and introduced their products for sale - products include honey, the special honeyed drink as well as horse bone powder. Could have done without the sales pitch, and have had more time with the history and culture.

If you've never been to a traditional Korean market, the Jeju Five Day Market is a wonderful introduction, and if you are an old hand at these sort of things, then you will enjoy Jeju's style. Pros: Roughly the size of a football field, there's a little of everything at this market. And every market is a little different too, so it stays interesting even over multiple visits (seasonal goods are fantastic here). Fruits, vegetables, herbs, roots, jams, honey, traditional medicines, gardening supplies (including seedlings); clothing, shoes, traditional crafts, a sprinkling of electronics now and then, kitchenware, furniture, rugs, and a whole host of things you won't recognize. It's truly a bizarre bazaar, and I am hopelessly in love with the sights, sounds, and smells of this style of capitalism that hearkens back to a time of more hooves and mouths than credit cards and smartphones. Go! Try everything! Buy everything! You'll love it!Cons: Sensory overload. Severe introverts should farm their energy for at least a day prior to going to this market. Expect to be shoved, bumped into, pushed, and in every other possible way have your personal space invaded. The shouting can be persistent, and the din is incredible. Trying to park your car can induce migraine headaches, and the traffic jams that lead up to the parking can be even worse. People here are generally honest, but I urge you to be extra vigilant when you buy perishables. More than once I've gone home with a great deal, only to have it go bad the same night. Also, check around for prices. Often you will buy something and then find a better version at a lower cost just a meter away. And finally, don't hesitate to haggle: the   foreigner price   rule is definitely in effect at this market.

If you've never been to a Korean public bath then there are some things you should know. First go in and pay - currently it's 6000 Won for the baths (segregated by gender) and 8000 Won for both the bathes and the   jimjilbang   (which is a unisex area filled with different hot rooms to enjoy a sweat lodge style experience). You can stay as long as you want and even sleep there. I would never suggest doing so however since even though this is a standard option for most Korean baths and they are arguably the cheapest place to sleep in Korea they are also loud sometimes crowded and generally pretty damned uncomfortable for sleeping. You will be given a set of shorts and a shirt. If you are large like me you can expect to have to cram yourself into them. Use the key provided to find a locker in your respective undressing area. Don't worry even though it doesn't seem like you should be naked in this area it's okay.From here you will go into the showering/bathing area. DO NOT get into any of the pools without first scrubbing yourself down. Soap is provided as well as some abrasive washcloths but you will need your own shampoo which you can buy in the changing area. Once you are clean you can enjoy a variety of different temperature pools and sauna options ranging from the almost freezing to the almost boiling. After you are finished soaking you can either shower again and leave or put on the shorts provided and go to the jimjilbang common area. Here you will find several different hot rooms including a traditional mud hut style outside that looks like a giant wasps nest. Some of these rooms are intense so work your way up to the higher temperatures don't stay in for too long and remember to drink lots of water. Food and beverages will be available in the common area so remember to stash some cash in your shorts before going to the jimjilbang. You can also relax on the floors in the common area watching some bad TV or just snooze. There are a few other nooks and crannies you can explore but this is a basic sketch of what you can expect. Once you're done at the jimjilbang you can go back for another shower and soak dry off enjoy some complimentary personal hygiene products (although I urge caution with their aftershave) get dressed and go home.  Yongduamhaesu Land is a decent example of a Korean bath. It's fairly clean and has some nice facilities. It's also pretty busy so expect high volumes of people especially tourists. Oh and for all you   foreigners   out there of non-Asian decent please expect an awkward amount of interest in your body especially those regions that you'd rather not have a room full of Koreans staring at. I know this is weird and to be perfectly blunt I wish they could be more circumspect with their curiosity but they don't really mean any harm. It's an unspoken obsession amongst humans - particularly men and especially Korean men - to compare genitals. Koreans just tend to be more obvious about it in ways that might signal either sexual interest or a punch in the mouth in non-Korean cultures. Have patience.

If you love trees and plants, caves, etc then you will enjoy Hallim Park. Great signage. Also the traditional village with thatched roofs was a treat. Had Mung bean pancake and fried pork for a tasty lunch. Great way to learn about Jeju and also a host of trees and plants from around the world. The volcanic caves were very interesting. Mr Song, the park's creator, had a great idea. Reasonable price as well. Highly recommend it.

If you like to explore and take pictures of traditional structures, this is the place for you. There are not a lot of explanations of what you are seeing but I don't think it needs it. There are some stores but not much. It is just like wandering around an old neighborhood. We went there on a taxi tour. I am not sure how easy it would be to access by public transportation.

If you have limited time in Jeju and like nature, visiting Hallim Park should be very high up on your list (if not your number one). Its beautiful and very varied. Palm trees, beautiful gardens, plants, flowers, birds, reptiles, 2 caves, a   traditional village   (where you can get a tasty traditional lunch) - its full of highlights and in 2-3 hours you can see so many different things. This is one of the most beautiful parks I have ever visited and I think everybody can find something they like there. If the weather is good, you can also combine the visit to Hallim Park with some time on a nice sandy beach just infront of the park.

If you are in the Seogwipo-city area and only a short time in Je-Ju this is a great find. A traditional house, a story of a great S. Korean artist, a nicely designed park and a street of small arty shops.

If it’s springtime?or even summer or fall-- that means it’s also time to think about visiting beautiful Gapado, or Gapa Island, which sits just off the southwestern tip of the Korean resort island of Jeju. ? Located some 5.5 km (3.42 mi.) offshore, Gapado is a quick ferry run from the port village of Moseulpo (maybe 20 min.)Gapado nearly got the distinction of being South Korea’s southern-most point, but that title went to nearby Marado.? Some tourists want to go there just to say they’ve been, but Gapado is noteworthy in its own right.? Gapada is home on its .84 sq. km? to about 250 residents.? The island has a picturesque school, a church and a Buddhist temple.? There are a couple Korean restaurants and small stores.? But, it’s a good idea to take bottled water and snacks with you, particularly if you plan to hike or bike all the way around the island.? You can bring your own bike, or perhaps rent one there.? Walking (Gapado has a 5k hiking trail that is part of Jeju’s famous Olle Course) or biking/electric scooter likely will be your only transportation choices, as there are no fossil-fueled vehicles on Gapado… But more about that in a bit.What makes it so special there?? Gapado offers spectacular views of the iconic mountain peaks or “sans” back to the north on Jeju, including Sanbangsan, Gunsan, Songaksan, Gogeunsan, Dansan and the Big Daddy of All Sans, Halla…the massive, central shield volcano that formed Jeju Island and the highest peak in South Korea.Equally impressive are Gapado’s golden-green barley fields, surrounded by traditional “batdam” stone agricultural walls.? The crop begins sprouting in late winter and reaches its full glory in late spring.? Gapado’s tradition of barley cultivation dates back to the 1840s and is celebrated annually with the Gapa Green Barley Festival. (Dates for 2015 are April 18- May 10.)Back to that transportation thing…well, barley is not the only thing green about Gapado.? Wind turbines, solar panels and other renewable, sustainable forms of energy are now being used on the island as part of a plan to make it one of the world’s first carbon-free islands, maybe THE first…. Summing up:? Good points:? outstanding natural beauty and photo ops in all directions; fresh air; clear aqua-hued seas that reveal black lava rocks; abundant hiking; colorful neighborhoods festooned with murals, recycled art and traditional Korean cultural artifacts;? site of annual Gapa Green Barley Festival? (April 18-May 10, 2015)Be sure to have on hand:? bottled water and small snacks; comfortable shoes; sunblock;? sunglasses; and a hat that won’t blow off easily; a stroller for very young children, layered clothing for coolish days.? There is little shade on the island, so be on guard against dehydration or sunburn on those hot or even excessively windy days.? Getting there:? Take an Intercity Bus from most points on Jeju Island to Seogwipo Main Terminal, and from there, a local bus to Moseulpo .? There is a short walk to the ferry from the busstop.? Ferries generally run twice a day, but as schedules and fares can change, it’s probably best to check for specifics through the Korean Travel Hotline: dial 1330 in country or outside Korea: +82-2-1330 or 1339 (Korean, English, Japanese, Chinese)

I was really impressed by this museum, designed by the famous Japanese architet Tadao Ando. The architecture of the building and the beautiful garden make this place worth a visit, but the collection is also really interesting. I really loved the collection artefacts from the late Joseon period an the special exhibition 'Carriage to Heaven' that shows sangyeo (traditional funeral bier) and kkokdu (small statues used as decoration for the sangjyeo). The joyous artwork of Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama were a nice extra on top of all that.Not to be missed when visiting Jeju.

I was looking forward to seeing the traditional/indigenous village but after a quick walk around we were marched into a hut ...after a brief introduction about this ancient village,then the hard sell began. Impressive products made from horse bones & horse oil - with almost magical values! No, I didn't buy anything.This is not a living village. I could only sight tour operators.

I visited here with several work colleagues.  We had a great time and laughed so much trying to make our way through this maze.  Built by a westerner and former professor over a number of years, the time, planning and care that went into making the park are all quite easy to see and appreciate.  It is beautiful there, very green and clean, and close to Manjang Caves, another iconic Jeju attraction.  Negotiating the maze took us about 45 minutes...longer than we thought...but we laughed our way through it.  Once you make it to the center, you can climb up to a platform and ring the   finder's bell.    Great for photo ops.  They also have some traditional Korean games just outside the end of the maze...fun to play if you never have.  At the snack bars, they offer delicious Jeju-brand ice-cream.  And as a BIG added bonus for my fellow cat-lovers, LOTS AND LOTS of mascot cats, belonging to the mazepark builder.  He is now a retired gentleman, known for his affinity for cats; journalists and business persons who go to meet with him in his office are likely to find both his desk and his person draped with one or more of his uniquely colored cats...black, orange, brown, white and grey.  A GREAT activity for families (although very young children may tire unless you take them in a stroller); couples; and colleagues...good team-building exercise:  Who can lead us OUT of here?  LOL  You'll enjoy it.

I quite enjoyed this place. It takes a while to walk around so don't go if you are in a hurry. If you take your time there is plenty to see, ancient tombs, traditional housing/tools, stone statues, giant stone towers, etc. The museum was also good and I learnt a bit about volcanic rock formation that I hadn't seen before.

I live quite close to this beach and really love it. On days ending on 1 and 6, there is a traditional market which is nice. Many restaurants to choose from, as well as an Olive Young, Spanish restaurant, Starbucks, etc however I prefer buying CU drinks and sitting in the sand. Sunset is AMAZING here.

I like to explore super markets in different cities and different countries. It's a good way to see what people are eating. Sometime when I have the courage, I will tried some of the local food. Dongmun Market is one of the popular traditional markets in Jeju. It is big, clean and colourful. They sell all kinds of stuff, like fruit, fresh or dry (some in gift boxes), vegetables, dry mushrooms, herbs, spices and fresh or dry sea food. There are some restaurants ready to serve you. They even sell clothing there. We walked around and took photos, but no one came to pressure us to buy stuff, I like that.Happy Travelling!
I like the ume flower garden, canola flower field, mini traditional folk village and greenhouses of cactus.

I had visited the Korean Traditional Folk Village in Seoul but was very curious to see this one since I had heard a lot about it. I drove there with a hired Taxi, and the driver /guide and I were greeted by some Villagers near the gate. They were very curious about where I was from so we spoke a bit with my guide interpreting for us. I find it interesting that this village is still inhabited. The one in Seoul is not. However, I prefer the experience I had in the one in Seoul because it showed me more aspects of the Korean traditional life.

I guessed many have mentioned that this was a typical market and I do not think they were wrong. However, it really depends the reason for your visit. If you are here to try cheap and good raw and fresh seafood (eg: raw fish slices for 10000won only), OR to try a variety of local food (eg: Sundae aka blood sausage, traditional fishcake stick, Kimbap, fresh Jeju orange juices, different types of kimchi, korean rice cakes, croquette, Tteokbokki, hotba, Modeumjeon - where they eat during new year and jeons, OR to purchase souvenirs and snacks for your family and friends then you are at the right place! It was also cheaper to purchase dried goods like ikan bilis and kelp in the market than supermarkets.We were at Seogwipo Maeil Olleh Market before coming to this market and we found that stalls that sell Jeju's souvenirs and local snacks such as Jeju crunch chocolate were cheaper in this market. The shop owners also gave us a handful of other snacks to try after our purchase in hope that we would be back for more. In Summary, this was a good place to try many local food at a smaller amount and a place to purchase affordable snacks for gift at a cheaper price.

I find it as an average, nothing special ... better to walk around outside the stone park,the surrounding is quite nice with traditional hall nice traditional look toilet (no hot water, water is icey cold) I came last month (early May)

Horses are a big part of the Jeju culture  and Jeju Horse Park is a pretty cool place. Its museum includes many photographs  artifacts and a video telling the story of the Jeju   ma    or pony  which is descended from the ponies brought to the island by Mongol invaders. The island was considered a good place to raise horses  and the Mongols used it as such. At the park  you can also ride the horses. There is a great giftshop with lots of local handmade items. Children or even adults can make related crafts in an activity room. The building itself is round like a ger  the traditional nomadic tents used by the Mongols. The top deck includes a fabulous 360-degree view of the   oreums   (small cinder-cones or parasitic volcanoes) that literally ring the area of the park. Inside the railing  an artist has painted the oreums  along with their names. So  you can know exactly which oreums you are viewing. There are also some actual Mongolian gers (also known as yurts in other nomadic cultures). I believe tourists can actually spend the night in one of the gers. One thing to consider: If you want to visit  you must either have your own transportation or go with someone who does. It's kind of far from anywhere  and bus service may not operate in that area. Likewise  taxis don't just happen by. But  it is a beautiful area and interesting for the entire family We visited in the spring  and there were also lots of colorful wildflowers. Plan to spend a few hours there  especially if you will ride the horses.

History of traditional Korean Tea and a brief introduction to tea in general. You'll have a chance to walk about the surrounding tea garden. Also a chance to saviour a variety of green tea and cakes. Catered for tourist it's not exactly a place for sipping cuppa and reflecting on   Zen   but it's green tea for what it's worth to appreciate.

Have you ever seen a more mouthwatering set of pictures? ㄴ Today we are enjoying a famous traditional dish from Jeju Island, Black pork.  Thick cuts of juicy pork belly, cooked to a smokey crisp just how I love it. Alone the pork belly is enough to eat by itself and a side of rice. But we're not here to be basic, you either go big or go home, enjoy the side dishes that come with every meal.  For example bean sprouts, ssamjang is known as a Korean bbq dipping sauce. It was mildly spicy and salty flavor with nutty fragrant. And, most importantly it compliments well Korean pork belly bbq. Lastly the infamous cabbage Kimchi, enough of a kick but not too much where you cant taste the perfect blend of food. A perfect combination, Bon-Appetite!

Hallim Park is Jeju largest theme park with various botanic gardens. It was created in 1971 by Mr Bong-kyu Song who loved his homeland to welcome visitors to Jeju Island. The park is located at the west side of the island. You may reach there by taxi or taking bus 702 from the Jeju city outer city bus terminal and stop at Hallim.VIPs from China, Finland, Japan, North Korea and the US had visited the park.Inside this tropical park, it has several botanic gardens with beautiful pot plants, flowers & common Jeju stone statues, a bird garden where you can see white peacock and the unique larva caves (Hyeopjae and Ssangyong Caves). It also has  the Dolharubang Restaurant which serves Jeju's traditional foods, the Palm Tree Restaurant to serve freshly made seafood and the Herb cafe to serve coffee and herb beverages.A good place for a day visit  by the family.

Hallim park is a good place for a day of relaxation and enjoyable experiences.The entrance fee is KRW10,000. You will be provided the map of the park.The park divided into 9 different themes. We didn't have chance to explore all of it.There is a beautiful cascading waterfall. If you are pressed for time, it is better to visit this place first.Hallim Park also have traditional-styled houses as folk village in Jeju.Within the park,there is also a plant nursery. Different species of flowers are found here.Throughout the park, there are numerous sculptures, among others the famous Stone Grandfather.Other than that, it have Bird Garden, Hyeopjae & Ssangyong Caves

Hallim Park features an extremely interesting cave complex quite unique as it has been dug by lava, a traditional Korean village, beautiful waterfalls, a bonsai garden and a section with creative sculptures. The price is very affordable and you can also visit the beautiful beach opposite the park while you're there. Worth a visit if you have spare time on your hands as it is quite far from the main attractions.

Halla mountain can be hiked in 3-5 hours easily. I have hiked the Seongpanak Trail (on the east side)  and the Gwaneumsa Trail (on the north side). These are the two trails that go all the way up to the summit. If you are fit, these runnable, but Geaneumsa trail especially gets very steep at the end. Get to your trail of choice early to miss the crowds, and also note that the half way points of each trail close around 12 (depending on the time of year it is sometimes 12:30). Een when it is foggy it is beautiful, but, of course, it is best when you can see clearly down to the crater lake and across off of Jeju to the ocean. Pack a lunch and enjoy it on top of the mountain! (Or instant ramen is the traditional food to pack).My favorite time to go is in winter when the top of the mountain is covered in a few feet of snow! Make sure to bring crampons for your shoes (simple ones are OK, you aren't hiking K2!)

Haenyeo literally means, 'Women of the Sea' and this museum pays tribute to the historical significance of this dying profession.  Solely carried on the backs of women on this island, these incredible ladies have carried their over 400 year old craft into the 21st century where instrumentally built the economic foundation for many of the Jeju natives.  Mothers who passed on their skills and knowledge of the sea to their daughters ensured that this lineage would endure the centuries of time.  However, as the world faces rapid changes and economies - the Haenyeo divers are slowly becoming a ghost of the past.  Recently recognized as an UNESCO intangible Cultural Heritage in 2016, tremendous efforts are in place to preserve this historical tradition.  A bonus of a visit to this museum is a trip to Sunrise Peak where there is a traditional Haenyeo performance.  (admission fee required)However - enroute to Sunrise Peak is the opportunity to meet a handful of Haenyeo divers!  What a thrill to visit with them in their modern 'bulteok' - warming huts.  Of all the sights of Jeju - this is perhaps the one that represents the very backbone of this amazing culture!This is definitely a 'must see'

From Segiowipo (Jangung rotary) the park can be reached in a little over an hour on the 231 bus which will drop you at the front of the park.   Fare 1200krw. Park admission is 5000krw. I spent 2.5 hrs here doing course 1 and 2. I think you might enjoy it more if you were an artist but I liked it all the same. The stone museum, which is the first stop on course 1 tells you all about how lava rocks are formed, their different types and would be a geologists dream. After that you'll walk around the park and see the different stone sculptures, most of which are natural,  some manmade. There are also a couple of replica traditional jeju houses and local pottery too. The Obaek gallery has some driftwood on display along with 1 hall of art but it is mostly empty. I thought there would be more info on the local traditions and how they lived but the park is still a work in progress. Its not due for completion until 2020. Rug up because it seems to be colder here than other areas of the island and you will be outside most of your visit. Recommend you go on a sunny day as this area gets very heavy fog too.

For only $10 (10,000 KW) you can spend an afternoon wandering around a carefully manicured small park that exhibits outdoor glass work. As you walk in there is a place to watch professional glass blowers blow bottles in the traditional way, and if you are taking a school group there, the kids can have ago at making something, and then return the next day to pick up their handiwork. After that you follow the path around the exhibits until you get to the other end.In this mainly outdoor museum, there are glass plants, flowers, and an eclectic collection of glass made curiosities that make a very pleasant way to spend a couple of hours. There is a small cafe in the middle of the exhibition, and the gift shop just before you exit. The bathrooms are at the entrance exit, so go before you start!

Every kind of locally caught fish and produce can be found in the Dongmun Market, as well as some imported items.  Don't miss out on getting a box of mandarins or Hallabong oranges.  Try the kiwifruit, too.  It's also a good place to sample Jeju's   street food   made by local vendors.  You can find all sorts of clothes and many household gadgets, accessories, rain shoes, Korean quilts, souvenirs...you name it, it's most likely in the market.  You can visit Dongmun during the day or at night.  Nearby, you can also see Sanjicheon Square, where local performers can also be found playing, singing or dancing for tips.  Some local seniors and maybe a few homeless persons frequent the area, adding to its   color.    The square is by a small tidal inlet, and features a quaint railing with traditional Korean characters on the railing.  Do check it out!

Even in March, Udo is beautiful--and in March, there are few visitors. When we were there, haenyo were out at low tide collecting seafood among the lava rocks, banging the rocks to bring them out. We stayed at a traditional hotel (thin mattresses on heated floor) near the lighthouse on the main road. Eat al fresco at the nearby restaurant across from the healing-stone throne is and check out their fresh   ginseng of the sea   (slices of a raw sea-cucumber-like animal). On the mainland, be sure to check out tiny Gangjeong Village, on the southern coast just west of Seogwipo, where villagers and Jeju priests are braving police, the navy, Hyundai, and Samsung 24/7 as they protest a huge naval base being foisted upon them. The mayor was jailed a few days ago for chaining himself around the neck to a rafter, when police rampaged and tore down protesters' headquarters, replacing it with boulders to prevent reconstruction. The protesters are very friendly, by the way. It's on the Ollie hiking trail, where it crosses over the Gangjeong River and passes the gates of the   destruction   site. A beautiful waterfall meets the sea and can be viewed by taking a path on either side of the bridge. Poonglim Resort is nearby, with full spa and small steam bath facilities.

dongmun si chang is a place for traditional item shopping. They sell seafood, fruits, chocolate souvenirs, meat and vege. I have no idea about the pricing as i didn't ask much. Just manage to get some orange chocolate as souvenirs because it close at 8pm korea time. Then i visit Junggak underground shopping centre which will close at 10pm.
Cute traditional  houses with Korean villages  culture. Nice scenary  for photos  taking.  If u like  to see ancient culture,  this is a place to visit

caves, bonsai trees, birds, nice gardens, restaurant in traditional style, and very well maintained area, the owner really has a passion to gardening and pride for his homeland. worth to visit at anytime, in summer you can also enjoy magic sandy beaches on the other side of the park

Built on a reclaimed land-fill site, this vast area of pathways, statues, displays, museums and traditional villages is very worth a visit if on Jeju. From the impressive stone structures and flat basalt 'floor' at the entrance of the park, I was blown away by the vast array of statues that are displayed, explained and on show in this area. There is ample car parking that is only a short walk form the entry way. A small fee is required and then you are free to wander the area that included a massive and spectacular 2 store (below ground) museum that outlines the geographic development of Jeju along with many interactive displays, a short film with subtitles, examples and galleries of 'stone art'. A gift shop of course, provided a range of traditional and specific items and there are amenities spread throughout the part. Water features, a traditional village, an art gallery and a vast array of stone sculpture will give you hours of things to view and read as you wander through the park In my humble opinion, not to be missed!!!

Bonte Museum was designed by Tadao Ando who designed scores of museums (including the Suntory Museum in Osaka) in Japan so the building itself is very photogenic.? The complex is divided into five galleries with one of them permanently housing two works by Yayoi Kusama, Pumpkin and the Infinity Mirrored Room (each visitor gets two minutes inside).? One gallery is dedicated to Tadao Ando’s meditation room while the rest of the? artwork inside rotates.? The other three galleries were pretty bland with one dedicated to Korean traditional crafts and the other two dedicated to temporary exhibitions.? Each gallery is relatively small with the entire museum taking a little over an hour to check out.? The spacious surrounding area is a nice spot to chill after checking out the art if the weather is nice and despite the steep admission, it was still a worthwhile stop.

Beautiful scene to be seen. Very natural. 20,000 stones of different verities. Natural as traditional village houses in India. Toilet facilities are everywhere. Very clean. Dogs and cats are not allowed.Water fountain is there. very good place for peace, health and meditation.Thanks.

As reviewed here, the first 10-15 minutes guests are taken on a tour to the various stations to see how traditional living in korea were. However the sales pitch on honey and several other product seems to have nothing really to do with the traditional farm life (or not obvious)... Do note the sales is not compulsory, but often, guests are 'pressured' into buying something by other guests..

Actually like the other ones, I felt quite surprise at the my first visits since last year 2011. The guide showed me that I were in the bottom of the slope, she pointed to the tree lines along  the side of the road and truly, it has made me believe what she said. Some one said it caused by a natural magnetic power (as above), other one assumed by the trick of the sun's lighting a man nearly lying face down to the road parallel to look forward to the starting point... others wisely poured the water to see the flows .... A very small traditional village attraction with free guide who can speak Mandarin. Very limited traditional houses to look at. No big deal. The attraction is apparently made famous by a TV series that filmed there. Nothing much to see but the guide took great efforts in explaining about each mini-attraction in the village. We ended up in a hut being given explanations on the local products they were selling (e.g. local honeys, herbal health drinks, horse bone powder, horse creams). We were not forced to buy but given that the tour was free, we were obliged to buy stuff that we could easily find for lower prices as the markets, especially Dongmun Traditional Markets in Jeju City.

A traditional market which sells a lot of Jeju Oranges, jeju chocolates, seafoods (e.g. Fish, abalone, etc), pork, orange juices and many more.. the price of the chocolates is the same as any other stores outside. The price of the other products are also reasonable.You can visit this market and have a feel of their largest traditional market in Jeju. I went there with my friend before 8pm but some of the stores had started cleaning and preparing to close the shop. The market is open till 9pm (if I am not wrong).

A traditional market situated in Jeju City that gives you a real and authentic taste of the local lifestyle in Jeju. It sells a wide range of local produce and goods. Buy all your local souvenirs such as hallabong orange, jeju chocolates and snacks here! The shopkeepers will toss in freebies (they call it   service  ) as well! It is near the black pork street which is also worth the visit.

A local will show you around and explain about traditional living in korea, but you cant really enter the houses. They will end the short tour by selling their products. I bought the honey and it was pretty tasty.. There was literally only 2 bathroom stalls so expect long lines.

A local has fulfilled himself a dream. He moved ground to this place and built this park with areas for Bonsai, azalees, palm trees, a natural lava tunnel, traditional houses, strangely formed lava rocks etc.The stop here is part of  a bus tour tio the Western part of the Island.
A great variety of exotic trees & flowers, marvellous birds, unusual sculptures,charming waterfalls, traditional symbols of  Jeju Island.  Beautiful inspiring day.

A great museum well set out, very informative. Theres a short film, in English or Korean. Then a self directed tour of museum. Exhibits are well laid out with English translations. I would love to have had a translation of the interviews with the Haenyeo   women of the sea  . There is also a Haenyeo trail from the museum, taking in some of the traditional places the women divers used including the Bulteoks. You would need quite a lot of time to do both museum, park, and trail.

A good place to go shopping and grab something to eat. You can find from cheap street food to fine dining Jeju traditional restaurant! Also, if you are a fruit lover like me, you can find all kinds of fruits in a reasonable price!

With Snoopy Garden’s steep entrance fee it initially didn’t make my itinerary. But the good reviews were consistent and friends also highly recommended the Charles Schulz’s Peanuts themed museum and garden. The indoor museum part was the highlight for me which had explanations about every main Peanuts character and several comic clips that span over Schulz’s 50 years of drawing them. The old newspaper clippings old toys and old books were also cool to look at. There are dozens of great photo spots which can create some major bottlenecks on crowded days. The garden had about half a dozen themed areas (including my favorite Charlie Brown’s baseball field) that are pretty vast and would have been a lot more pleasant to walk around in cooler weather. We skipped the cafe that charged a criminal 8500 won for a lemonade. I’m not sure that the high price of admission is justified but this is a well maintained attraction(which is refreshing considering the high number of run down museums and small theme parks in Jeju) and the quality of the displays are of superb quality. Adults and children both also fans and non-fans of Peanuts both would enjoy the visit here.

While its really small against Western style theme parks we enjoyed an afternoon on the rides.  Also if you arw a US military service member or have a military ID (they don't know the difference between a dependent or soldier) you can get an amazing deal.  It was 9k won for 2 day combo pass for the theme park and the water park!!! Which is usually 39k won.  There is also a discount if ypu are staying at one of the resort hotels.  The park was clearly designed by someone who has visited and studied the Disney parks specifically Tokyo Disney Sea.  Which isnt a bad thing just needed to be mentioned.  This was our 2nd visit and have never had to wait in a line for the rides.  Also the rides are enjoyable the staff is friendly & helpful and the park is very well maintained.

We walked through the Sex and Health Museum and took some crazy pictures!  It is a large museum with many different themed areas.  There is a sex education hall showing sexual positions differences in male and female pregnancy and more.  Other halls have sexual movies playing displays of sexual cultures from all over the world lifelike sex dolls and the craziest statues of things like a humongous penis.  Overall we enjoyed the museum had many good humored laughs and got some funny pictures.

We visited this last for the day at Jungmun Resort since this opened till rather late (~8+pm). Last entry should be around 7pm since it would take you around 1 1/2 - 2 hours if you're gonna snap alot of the photos inside. If you are already inside Jungmun Resort and are travelling in groups you can take a cab to this place since it would not cost much and you can save the hassle of walking. The paintings inside are really cool and we had a fun time snapping photos away. Effects came out rather cool on the photos. There are several sections in the museum and each sections has its own theme. Definitely worth a visit and we really didn't regret it. Initially we intended to spend only 1 hour in the museum since we really rushing off to other places in the night. We ended up spending 2 hours there. So do equip yourself with a camera and of course have someone with you to take photos for you.

We spent some fun hours here luckily the weather was beautiful and I'd suggest to visit when it's sunny so the place can really shine. Could be better maintained but we liked it regardless. So what's to see here? Installations of famous landmarks and a tiny Korean village (which is more like few houses really). I wouldn't call this a theme park I'd say it's a park with an interesting and enjoyable theme without toys. I think most parks and museums in Jeju share one common problem: the staff seems to be nonpresent and there's a serious lack of catering service. No coffee shops restaurants or they're either closed. I think this place had something but I think it was closed. Either way I think it's worth visiting if you happen to be around and the surroundings are pretty too.

Very nice place and worth a visit. It will require you around 2 to 3 hours to visit the entire park. Train ride is nice too. Beautiful scenery. Love how the park or each train stop has different theme. It maybe very hot during sumer time
Very cute themepark to while away a good 1-2 hours. Good for summer when it's too hot outside. The rooms are separated into various different themes. Particularly good for silly selfies!!

Ultra modern building houses green tea related information and displays.But you really want to snack on green tea themed ice creams or others and walk in the garden of lush green tea shrubs.As garden is outdoors you want to avoid visiting during rain showers.

Tulips are great. But cherry blossom are ending. The tropical garden is very impressive. If only the other parts of the garden were better maintained. I would have rated this place 5 stars. The caves was very interesting. From hot garden to cold caves. The follow by waterfall. It?s very nice transition. One must spend about 3-4 hours to fully explore this garden and use the guide to walk through the garden. I really enjoyed walking this garden with many different theme. Keep up the good work and hopefully with your increased price you can do better maintenance.
This place has several themed hiking trails. You can choose one of them according to your allotted time. You can walk comfortably under the shady trees. I recommend this place is a must-see in Jeju.

This park is huge! it is divided into different areas with different themes. It has a great variety of plants and birds. There are also two underground tunnel caves which enrich the overall visiting experience. There is also an area with seasonal flowers.  Great spot for photo-taking. Highly recommended for family with children. Allocate at least two hours visiting time here.

This is better known as Jeju Love Land Park and I thought it was hilarious! Everything that could be penis shaped is penis shaped it is full of sculptures pictures dioramas. I wouldn't call it educational or a museum but a sex themed amusement park and indeed I was amused!

This attraction is not theme ark but a large garden. In my opinion station 1 and 4 is the best area for taking photo. Down from the train at Station 1 and take a walk aroud 15 minutes to station 2 and take lots of picture :)

There is nothing exciting with the Jeju Chilsung Fashion Street. It is a series of open-air pedestrian-only road lined with boutiques. The stores were familiar such as Starbucks New Balance Spyder MLB Tommy Hilfiger Crocs and Adidas although there are some designs that are available here that are not yet available in the Philippine market.The place was supposed to be part of the Jeju Winter Festival. Indeed there were a number of Christmas-themed displays although they were nothing compared to how lavish the Christmas displays in the Philippines are.I only strolled around the area then went to the Dongmun Market nearby. The Jungang Underground Shopping District is also close?봞s it was winter it was more comfortable shopping at the heated underground location of Jungang that it was in Chilsungro. Also the items sold at Chilsungro are from brands that are more known internationally (and thus are more expensive) than what is available at Jungang.

There are several Alive Museums in Korea and Singapore.  Each features a series of themed scenes for trick-art photos.  You can pose as directed for each scene and create a funny memorable photoThis one is located in the Jungman Tourist Resort area on the southern side of Jeju Island.  We ended up going there on a rainy day when it was just too blustery to be on the beach.  Unfortunately everyone else had the same idea and it was too crowded.  We had to wait so long to take photos that we ended up not getting very many views for our memory book. I think we only took about a half-dozen.  It was so crowded in fact that it was even difficult to walk.  And it is a big place!  There are also interesting photo ops outside the building such as with various types of vehicles and statues.  I think the Alive Museums would offer a better service to visitors by following the system used by museums for special exhibits:  issue a limited number of tickets for a specific time period allowing one group to move through to a certain point before starting the next.  Really the best part about our visit is that we purchased a combo entrance ticket purchased there for 12000 Korean won  (about $10 USD) that allowed us to visit the nearby African Museum which was FANTASTIC and well worth the time spent there.  So if you go to the Alive Museum try to go early or pick a sunny day.  Or if you don't mind crowds and lots of jostling about it can be part of your rainy-day beach retreat.  Either way get the combo ticket!

My family and I chose the Alive Museum over the Trick Eye Museum because the former is larger and has more art pieces. Furthermore we chose to go in the evening after dinner so that we don?셳 have to jostle with the daytime crowd. However the disadvantage of the night visit is that the karting (carting) activities were already closed at 5 pm. Moreover it was too dark to take any photographs with the outdoor sculptures in the French themed garden. But it?셲 okay because our primary objective was to have a good time inside the Museum which we did. Getting there and Fees: We drove to the Alive Museum (GPS coordinate/code 8050888) and reached there at about 7pm 2.5 hours before Museum closing time of 9:30pm. Parking is free at the huge car park. Entrance fees to the Alive Museum is 10000 won for adults 9000 won for teenagers and 8000 won for children. If you rent a car check whether there are available discounts on the entrance fees and karting on the discount booklet (we used those from the Hertz discount book).The Museum:  Depending on your time spent at each art piece and the number of visitors present (who would jostle with you for the right to pose and take photos) you would need at least 2 hours to ?쐏articipate??in all the art pieces inside the Museum. It is very easy to become so engross that you lose track of time! And don?셳 worry about how to pose because there?셱e instructions and explanations written in Korean Mandarin (Chinese) English and Japanese on how to pose. If you are going by yourself I recommend you bring a tripod along or you could take selfies (although most photos have to be taken beyond the selfie distance) or you could keep asking other visitors to take your photos.We leisurely spent a lively 2.5 hours (7-9:30 pm) inside the Alive Museum which was just enough to view and take photographs and selfies of most of the art pieces. I say ?쐌ost??because there are a few paintings of adult themes which are not suitable for my children. Anyway we almost had the entire museum to ourselves except for 6 other visitors! So we unreservedly and hilariously pose at most of the 3-D art and paintings without feeling shy and without anyone looking at us. As a result we were among the last to leave the Museum.Of the 4 categories of art inside the museum ??trick art digital art objet art and Provence art (sculpture art is outside the museum) ??my favourite are those in the trick art section. Trick art is a perspective technique which makes use of optical illusions so as to enable visitors to interactively ?쐃nter??as the main character into seemingly three-dimensional realistic paintings and artworks with the visitors eventually having a good laugh at their ?쏿dventure??  I particularly liked the 3-D illusions of the parachute standing on the bridge over the molten lava and the hanging onto a nail at the side of the building. We also enjoyed the Provence art section which is a pastel-coloured fairy tale village with bears and dogs donning period costumes.We had a truly unforgettable experience with plenty of amazing photographs and fun with optical illusions. So could you!

In Jeju  we had the opportunity to visit the Jeju Art Museum & Glass Castle  which is a theme park featuring an exhibition hall  garden and models made entirely of glass. If you are big fan of the Korean variety show Running Man (?곕떇留?  you will enjoy walking around Ilchul Land. Ilchul Land is quick to play up on the connection for fans as there are various signboards placed around the attraction showing you exactly where certain scenes took place. Great for taking photos to show that you have been there!For regular visitors/tourists  Ilchul Land is more of like a very well maintained outdoor park  with lush and verdant landscaped scenery including bonsai plants  palm trees and even miniature waterfalls. However  the highlight for me was the natural underground cave/tunnel  which you can explore - do go all the way to the end (until you reach the roped off area) and mind your head as it is a bit low in parts. There are some carvings and statues placed inside the caves  whereas I would have preferred that it was left in its natural state. If I remember correctly  it was about a 10mins stroll all the way in.
