Jeju Folk Village Museum as it appears on map for Jeju is on the coast and is a must do for history and culture buffs. There are hands on exhibits that kids and adults can participate and use around the village. The park and museum is large and takes 2 to 3 hours at least. Perhaps longer to see everything without rush. We were quite impressed by the size the crafts people making products and the exhibits throughout. There are ample restrooms snack shops and Korean traditional products sold in the gift shop. There is also a restaurant on premise.The Jeju Folk Village attracts students from all over Korea as well as tourists from other countries. I highly recommend the park. There are beautiful floral blooms as well as animals photo opportunities and lots of traditional Korean history and culture to learn about. Well worth the price of admission. Plan to spend half a day here. Arrive early to avoid the crowds. There are some great gifts and candies to be found around the village including the traditional Korean taffy near the Hanbok photo place and the gift shop.

Jeju Folk Village is not very big and not small as well but it effectively demonstrates the history of Jeju tradition from the 1890s. Different types of villages were located systematically. While walking through different houses and villages it feels like visiting a real movie shooting studio. Everything looks clean and real just like somebody still leaving there. The real animals and bird kept makes it even more alive village. Some of the life-size dummies kept there to display the old traditions and clothes were remarkable. The posters in from of few houses indicated that those were indeed used in making popular movies or TV dramas based on the old lifestyle.Besides there are various exhibition halls performance hall dram shooting sites poultry farms etc. which make it even more interesting. People can also even enjoy various folk games. It actually not only allow people to observe the traditional Jeju lifestyle during the 1890s but also allow people to get experience by playing folk games wearing traditional Korean dress etc. Thus it is recommended to visit this place during a visit to Jeju.

I went there with my friends  thinking it was an aquarium  and I do not recommend this place at all! What they're doing to this beautiful animals is pure cruelty. We can obviously see the intensive training  the abuse and the fear these poor animals (monkeys  dolphins) are going through. There was a baby dolphin completely lost and unable to do the show in this tiny tank  but they forced the adults to do the show again and again  until the baby succeeded it. The baby ended up banging his head on the wall.. It was just unbearable to watch. After that  no food in return for the others. The animals shouldn't be here  and treated like that. I'm surprised no one launched a petition against this facility yet. Its just pure sadness  cruelty. It's not something children should see... I do not recommend it.

I visited this aquarium with my family on New Year?셲. I had high hopes for it since it was rated as one of the top 10 world?셲 best aquariums in the world. I saw a lot of kids grabbing the sharks by the tail grabbing them out of the water to carry them across the room and throw them into another tank. I was disappointed that such a conservation-based aquarium did not place staff at the touch tanks to make sure the visitors learn how to respectfully handle animals. However besides that a great place to learn about marine life and support Jeju tourism & conservation.

review: Gardens were not well maintained (except bonsai garden good) but it broke my heart to see the conditions of the animals in captivity. Completely turned me off.

Exotic Jeju Island is known for many things: the majestic Hallasan--the massive shield volcano that formed the island and the highest point in South Korea; its mandarin groves; persimmon-dyed galot fashions; the sturdy Jeju ma horses  descended from the ponies of Mongol invaders; tasty black pork; and the iconic haenyeo women divers. But most visitors would not expect to find a Museum of African Art there. And  it's pretty darn good! Located in a massive structure modeled after the mud-brick Great Mosque of Djenne  the museum offers photo-ops galore in its Safari section  although the animals are of the stuffed variety. Very popular with children and couples. The upper floors house a respectable collection of African artifacts and photographs by Kim Jung Man. There is also a great gift shop. But  I have saved the best for last...the live performance of African folk music and dance. The group  Zalia from Senegal  featured lots of drumming  and audience members also got a drumming lesson and a chance to play along on one song. All in all  a quality experience...and a surprising one.

Could have spent half a day here. Gardens were beautiful. The lava caves were nice to walk through to break up the heat! Interesting animals throughout.  Ran out of time and missed seeing the water gardens.  Great way to spend a day outside. Especially enjoyed the bonsai garden.

If there was no performance  I could not award high marks.

You can even get a teddy to propose marriage to you.Teseum should not be confused with Teddy Bear Museum located in Seogwipo (near Alive Museum), a more 'serious' museum.
Working hours from 8AM (or 9?) till 5PM.Spend 2-3-4 hours there, many flowers (in season), animals, folk village inside, two interesting caves. Just nice! :)

When visiting other countries I realize the treatment of animal standards may differ, but I at least look for animals to be happy. This falconry “center”was bittersweet. Some of the animals had wonderful enclosures, but the birds of prey were treated very inhumanly. The same birds of prey/owls were tied to stands for the whole 3 hours we were there, with no food or water, in the blaring sun, with no supervision as people crowded and tried to touch them to the point they would flinch or try to fly away, only to be yanked by their chains. Their inhumane treatment brought tears to our eyes. At the far part of the center, we came upon their enclosures, cages about 5 x 5 x5 feet wide, where other birds of prey were chained, with little place to move and absolutely no enrichment toys.? This is unacceptable. There was a raccoon in a small enclosure with no enrichment toys, solely used for tourists to take selfies with. Last but not least, a pair of Coaty were also in a small enclosure. Their baby was on display in a small cage by the gift shop with no water. This “Center” does have some acceptable enclosures for fowl, rabbits, budgies, and the alpaca interaction was amazing, but surely they can treat all their animals with dignity. While we were there, a macaw flew away into the surrounding trees. Clearly the parrot did not have an attached handler nor proper training for flighted birds.

Well, there were some photo-taking opportunities at the folk village (in the centre), a small waterfall etc. There's a bird section that comprised of a couple of parrots being kept in a small cage, and some other depressing-looking birds. Possibly some animal section (can't remember what they call it), with some big tortoises etc, and a lizard?Skipped the lava cave section as we had gone to see the other, more famous Manjang cave.Some tropical garden that was disappointing in terms of plant variety and   rare   factor. The bonsai garden is another major disappointment. We stepped into a big, totally un-aesthetic tent, with bonsai pots laid out on tables like goods in a warehouse. At the other end of the tent, a trail led out into what seemed like an unkempt garden with just trees, so we didn't bother to go check it out. We wanted to check out the flower garden but we must have missed the entrance path along the way - no signboard, no entrance and no sign of flowers (maybe they don't bloom in October?). We just did a cursory walk around the park and made our escape after an hour.I seldom recommend my own country to other travelers, but if anyone wants to visit an interesting garden, Gardens by the Bay in Singapore is so much better than the gardens at Hallim Park. I'm quite puzzled why this has such good reviews, but you can always visit it and be your own judge.

We were attracted by the promise from the literature that this was the only waterfall in Asia with 'debouches' into the ocean. Hmmm, you almost get the impression from above that some channel engineering has helped this along. Anyway, Wikipedia tells me that this claim is not quite correct. Anyway, we arrived as then had to purchase entry tickets. The stressed out man next to the ticket gate then seemed to think that we have not purchased the correct amount of tickets. We had. It was all the more puzzling because he was only 2 feet from where we bought the tickets. Maybe he was so bored he was asleep at the wheel. Or maybe it was because we were foreigners. Anyway, once that nonsense was resolved we headed down the steps, only to be stopped half-way down at yer another ticket check! Ridiculous, three check for a 1000-or-so won entry ticket. We thought we must be in for something very special. Alas not. Said waterfall falls a few score metres, generates a modest amount of spray and attracts thousands of people taking selfies of themselves and said insipid attraction. There are some older folk selling ghastly looking octopus slices by the rocks - poor animals (the octopus that is). We were not stopped for more ticket checks on the way out, thankfully. I suggest you just look at the photo on the web and go and do something more interesting instead.

We visited the Glass Castle with our grandchildren. They had a great time running through the forest full of glass flowers and animals, there was a multiple mirror room, It is a bit kiche, it shouldn't work but it does beautifully.

We hired a taxi for the day but this wasn't one of the place we wanted to go. The driver, Charles Cho, unilaterally decided we should stop at Sangumburi anyway. We're glad he did. We've been to Kintamani in Bali, but this crater is smaller and within a more scenic and lonely area. The surrounding mountains and farmland are serenely beautiful. One of the attractions here is a patch of tall reeds, but at this time of the year, they have not sprouted yet.The crater itself is supposedly valuable because of the unique plants and animals there, but for us casual visitors, it's a nice, green geographical feature.There are remains of tombs there, but no information on them.

We hiked up the gwaneumsa trail (shorter, steeper but more scenic route). Really glad we chose this route as there was far less people and the views were spectacular.We arrived to the trail head at 7am and paid the 1800 krw fee for parking. The trail head is clearly marked and there's a nice washroom that you can use before beginning the trek. The trail is well marked (there's no way you can get lost) and also well maintained.You reach the first rest stop around 3km into the hike. There's a very smelly washroom there (there's a better one at the next rest stop). You must reach the last rest stop by a certain time or else you won't be able to proceed. The time posted today was 1300 although it looked like the only barrier was a small chain that you could walk around so I'm not sure how enforced that rule actually is. After the final rest stop the trail goes downhill a bit then the steepest climb begins. The stairs don't seem to end for the last 2.7km!! The views are spectacular though. Once we reached the top there was so many people! Where did they all come from? The seonpanak trail. So glad we chose this trail instead.In the end it took us 4.5 to climb to the top of hallasan (with many rest/photo/food breaks) and another 3.5 hours to descend. I had 2L of water although I only drank about 1L. There were many bugs but I didn't seem to get any bites. There doesn't seem to be any dangerous animals out there although there are signs warning about boars.

We entered this park with great expectations - the gardens themselves are great, the bonsai area stands out as superb, and the Lava Caves offer some welcome respite from the heat.Everything in the garden was destroyed by the horrific and unacceptable conditions of the birds and other animals.  There was a smallish section with parrots, a few other birds, a monkey in a tiny cage and a few other small furry creatures.  It was filthy, some of the animals had no water, the temperature must have been 35 degrees.  There was one small animal that was clearly suffering greatly (in one of the cages with no water). I emptied the contents of my water bottle into it's water bowl, and reported its condition to a member of staff - who did nothing.We went on to see peacocks and ostriches, yes in slightly larger enclosures, but with no shade, no vegetation, and 13 peacocks in a tiny cage.  The birds were in obvious distress with obsessive grooming and clear skin infections.I've travelled all over the world, and been to many places like this and never, from the poorest, to the richest countries, have I seen animals kept in these conditions. I rarely, if ever, write reviews, but I am so angry at the conditions here, that it's important to be aware.The gardens are immaculate, the conditions of the animals are disgraceful, and should be an embarresment to whoever runs this organisation.Do not visit!

We came just after the rain stopped. Love the layout of the whole place. Instantly brings you back to the past there are real people - Craftsmen Painter Potter man on the respective   villages   with living animals - chicken black pigs goats horses. It is a nice experience. There are old   games   for you to try on. Saw traditional drummers along the way. You can have greater understanding on how the past Koreans houses based on their occupations - fisherman farmer locksmith painter. There are school police station & court house too. Few of the famous Korean dramas been shot here namely Jewel In The Palace.  A worker told us if we came on a non rainy day there will be more activities. Entrance fee is on higher side - 8000 Won/ Person but it is worth a visit.

We book a tour on line from the cruise ship before we arrived at the port. The tour included a visit to Seongeup Folk Village.  There was an admission fee to the village.  There are several walkways around the village. The walkways are well maintained and there are no steps to climb.  There are exhibits our old building, farming and animals.  There are clean restrooms along the walkways.

Visited the park in Feb. Pretty blooms of camellia and cherry blossoms. Unfortunately the park keeps animals such as rabbits and pigs. The rabbits are not kept in proper conditions. More appalling is a black pig show where pigs are made to run up a ramp and slide down a very steep 1.5 storey slope. Not sure how any one can find this   show   entertaining. What do children learn about such a performance where animals are at risk of injury for the amusement of humans? Ghastly place. Stay away unless taking Instagram pictures in fake settings are your thing.
Very beautiful park with flowers and cultures, exotic animals and a continued paved walk through a number of cool dark caves.

Unless you really really love Teddy Bears, this place is rather overpriced. At 8,000KRW per person, it gets expensive if you're in a group. And, they won't let you enter the gift shop without paying for a ticket. In the end, we found their gift shop not terribly different from the Safari Teseum (7,000KRW per person, but you can go directly to the gift shop). The Safari Teseum gift shop actually had more options (aka other animals for those who don't like stuffed bears).Still, if you really love Teddy Bears, you can make a day of it between the two places.

This was covered under our west course jeju tour.This is a large park with good bonsy trees ,lava caves and plants and animals and a old jeju village huts to show jeju culture.We can enjoy photography.If localite a good picnic spot.food shops available.

This was a very disappointing excursion. I've been to a number of international aquariums (Sydney and Cape Town - two of the best I've been to) and this one really pales in comparison - it's more a dolphin/seal show than an aquarium. We were shocked to discover that there doesn't even appear to be outdoor pools for the resident seals and dolphins! The animals did appear to be in good condition  but I'm not a big fan of animals putting on shows for humans  I prefer to just be able to observe them in their   natural   surroundings. The place seemed pretty popular with the locals though.
This place has variety of teddy bear. Upon entering, they have a zoo theme on the 1st floor. They have many zoo animals made of stuff toys. The 2nd floor is more of a theme section.

This park includes a variety of sights including two lava tubes, an aviary that includes a variety of peacocks, ostriches etc, a small traditional village, strange little rock people sculptures, and a very impressive botanical garden with outdoor sections around a pond and several green houses.   Some strange combinations in the outdoor section with large palms mixed up with various types of cacti and other random mixes of fabulous plant specimens from all over the world.  The greenhouse plants seem a bit more organized by regions or types (e.g., large cactus collection in one greenhouse; palms in another), with live animals interspersed between the plants (impressive boa and python collection, also some special turtles, and lizards such as nile monitors, iguanas, etc.).  In between plant viewing, I enjoyed a nice cool cactus juice relaxing in the herb bar.

This is just another roadside attraction that many people visiting Jeju stop by to see only because it is in the city proper. It is just a rock that could appear to look like any number of different animals.If your tour guide takes you out of your way to see this then you need a new tour guide because this rock is typical of any of the millions of rocks you run into along the seashore in Jeju.There are a lot of interesting things to see and fun places to go in Jeju but, this isn't one of them.

This is an authentic market which embodies local life on the island. It has so much to offer... There is an entire section devoted to the economy of the elderly, selling their goods and calling sweet encouragements to passerbys. There are regional fruits and veggies, artisan crafters, cloth and clothing sellers, seafood and fresh meats, animals, and a multitude of food trucks/stalls.This is the ideal market for immersing yourself in Jeju and Korean culture. It's open every day ending in 2 or 7: 2, 7, 12, 17, 22, 27thPictured: a pressure cooker used for puffing rice and corn, cooking beans, etc...

This is a lovely spot to visit. You can wander around the artists village enjoy the outdoor sculptures (kids will like the brightly coloured animals near the art shop/cafe) and then have a good look at the exhibitions inside.  There is a permanent one and a temporary one. The temporary one at present is about marine plastics and pollution. The work was really good especially the video work and created   man   by a young female Korean artist. Most impressive.The last Wednesday of the month entry is free but it's only 2000 won anyway I think. They have an English brochure and the lady at reception was very pleasant.

This is a difficult review to write - the vegetation and environment at Hallim Park is great but my visit was ruined by seeing the way that the animals of the park were being treated.Firstly the Macaw House, an extra 1000krw to enter a large, hot greenhouse full of gorgeous birds in tiny wire cages with no vegetation or shade from the scorching heat.  There was a small black skinned pig in a cage less than 1m long.  Some animals were showing clear signs of distress and in two cases I was seriously concerned that animals were suffering severe heatstroke in a room that was exceedingly hot (34C outside and hotter in the house).The 'Beautiful Bird Garden' is a similar story - birds in cages with little shade, clear mite infections and stress related loss of plumage.  There were a few lucky peacocks able to roam freely but most were in tiny pens (10-15 per pen).  The facilities were not well maintained and the lack of shade is shocking given the heat of the Jeju summer.This was the most depressing experience I've had in a park - I've seen better cared for animals in developing nations.  The conditions at this park bring shame on Jeju and the nation when it appears that plants are treated better than animals.  To make any claims the Hallim Park is an ecological park is rubbish based upon this!If you care for the welfare of animals I would strongly urge you to avoid and express you anger to the local government.

This is a cute collection of teddybears and other stuffed animals in a variety of settings (a castle, a safari, etc.), but it's not what I was expecting with the name   Teseum   (teddy+museum).  There's a very small display of older teddybears (mostly photographs), but the main attraction is the displays you can see in the pictures.  There must be thousands here, ranging in size from one inch or shorter to probably eight feet tall. I imagine kids would be in hog heaven, but some of the older people in our tour group said it was a waste of time.  My favorites were the safari and the teddybear versions of old paintings.

There are many many many uncountable (which may count but hei! not necessary man~) teddy bears inside and a lots of other animals dolls like brown bears, sheeps, monkeys, elephants, snakes, lions, tigers, etc. Me and my siblings are having a great photo time inside there. I feel lovely and joyful for all interior design which teddy bear had placed. Love this place much! Worth to visit once in lifetime.
The park is really big. Need at least 2 hrs to complete exploring. There's many things to see - from small animals, plants to caves. Great place to relax and enjoy the scenery.

The park has a beautiful array of flowers and other well kept vegetation. The animal displays are somewhat of an after thought, but are ok. This is a good place to spend time outdoors with friends, family, or in a tour group.

The interior was nice with teddy bears as the main characters. The costumes the bear was wearing was splendid. Other than bears there?s a mini safari displaying animals such as lions, bears, tigers etc. Overall, for adults you can finish visiting the place within 20 mins.

The grounds are amazing and beautiful. Different times of year you can see beautiful blooms like azaleas, hydrangeas, bougainvillea, etc. It?s definitely worth some time to see the natural beauty of the flora. The animal enclosures are very disappointing, because as a true natural park, you would expect better conditions for the animals. The caves are a good break from the sun and heat. They are a wet cave, so prepare to get drops on your head. They have a tour route that allows you to see everything. Recommend taking 2-3 hours to see everything.

The 5 day market is named because it opens every 5 days only. There are other 5 day markets in Jeju but this market is said to be the largest in Jeju with 1,000 over stalls. This market opens on the 17th and plus / minus 5 days before and after.Fret not if you missed the opening of this market. Because apparently the other 5 day markets are operate by the same stall owners. They rotate among the different markets and hence will be back to the same market after every 5 days.We went there on a morning and expected to spend the whole day there. But we were out in 2 hours.There are indeed many stalls in the market but many of them are carrying the same stuff. Clothings, household products, fruits and vegetables, kimchi, cooked food and of course Jeju mandarin oranges which are famous. Interestingly, pet dogs are sold alongside with fresh chickens. And ironically, there are stalls selling dog meat at the other end of the market.Same animal but different fate.We bought the famous mandarin oranges here although these are available at other places in Jeju as well. There are many similar-priced stalls selling this famous product in this market. We chose one of the varieties on display after sampling. It has a sweet aftertaste after the first tinge of sourness. The one we purchased is the 2nd most expensive type at $25,000 Won per 5 kg. There are other varieties at $30,000 Won per 5 kg and $15,000 Won per 10 kg etc.It?s a nice experience after all and I would say it?s worth a visit if you are in Jeju.

Teddy Bear Safari is the world?s first exhibition theme park with various real life-sized wildlife and marine stuffed animals and teddy bears. Moreover, you will also meet our teddy bears dressed in traditional clothes of countries around the world and as gods from Greek mythology. Lastly, some of our teddy bears will be dressed up as Korean celebrities whom you may be well aware of.
Take the afternoon and walk around this beautiful park and zoo. All different kind of plants, trees, flowers, and animals, this park is way better than it seems. Don't miss it!

So much fun!  I've been twice and would like to go back very soon.  In the spring, tulips everywhere!  So many different things to do and see here.  I fed the birds this time around and what joy.Note that some animals were not in the best shape (summer heat maybe).

Quite a small space... small 2 story building that looked big on the outside but its interior was small. I had actually envisioned the museum to be much bigger. Unless you've got kids, or you are really a fan of stuff bears and animals, I think this place can be missed.15 mins and we were out of that place.

People who visiting Jeju island is to see its nature (except those to Casino), Hallasan is a must go to me.  Together with the family, we opted for the route of Yeongsil (shorter though not to the top and unable to see the crater), where we could easily accessed by self driving from Seogwipo city.  Along the hiking, we experienced the sub tropical environment in the bottom, then a much cooler environment after 1.5km of steep uphill.  The view is great though not fantastic, we spotted few wild deers having grass in the mountain.  The first 2-3 km was quite steep but mostly on boardwalk and constructed staircases, the last 1-2 km was rather flat.We ended in the point with toilet and food supply and then back down on the same route, due to the last section was closed.  An interesting hiking day to experience different climate, weather condition, meet locals, spot the wild animal, and do physical exercise.

Not cheap entrance fee however there are lots of things to see.Even if you don't have much time, do not miss out their caves especially in hot days as it's so nice and cool inside. :)tiny little things to see everywhere and exotic animals as well.

Not a wordy person, but this truly is a must visit. A jeju local recommends it to me, totally fell in love with it. Not to swim but to explore, for kids to play with the fish and small animals on the rocks. Very safe.

My wife and I strolled around the market in  an early evening in mid-March 2017. The market was, as expected, already quite empty. However, the seafood stalls were still open and was quite a view. All sorts of fishes, clams, squids, octopuses and animals that I have never seen before were sold there.The whole market is huge, consisting of many sections selling various items, including fruits, vegetables, etc.Some street food stalls were still open too and we bought a cup of grilled octopus, sweet Korean pancakes and freshly-made orange juice. All were very nice.

My only concern with Hallim Park is the condition of some of the animals they have there. The 'cages' or 'presentation units' seem quite small for some of them, and some of the bigger birds didn't seem particularly happy. I don't want to give this an 'average' review because the caves are incredibly unique, the diverse array of trees and plants is also very special. But full disclosure, this place may not be for everyone.

My husband and I were staying in the Hallim area and our taxi driver mistakenly took us to Hallim Park. Especially since it was a bit chilly and an overcast day, the beautiful green houses and occasionally covered areas were a nice break from the weather. The park itself is nothing overly spectacular, but it has a little bit of everything with a nice mix of Jeju style to your typical botanical gardens type park. Plants, flowers, animals, exhibits, and fun!

My family and I spent about 45 minutes at this attraction on an early Monday afternoon, as our first stop of a Daepo Jusangjeolli Cliffs ? Jeongbang Waterfall ? Oedolgae ? Cheonjiyeong Waterfall itinerary. It is designated a Natural Monument and is part of the Global Geopark Network. Getting there & fees: When I keyed in GPS code of 7351000 and 7381521, it brought us confusingly to the Convention Centre and the car park of the Seaes Resort respectively. Thanks to the helpful staff of the Seaes resort, we followed the advice and drove past the Convention Centre and then looked out for a signage that indicated taking a right turn to a road that leads to the destination. Once there, we parked the car in the car park which charged a parking fee pf 1000 won. The entrance fee is 2000 won for adults & 1000 won for teenagers (youth) and children, and we used one of the lockers for free to keep our stuff.The Cliffs/Attraction: After paying the entrance fees, we walked past figurines of dolphins and a huge rock surrounded by the twelve animals of the Chinese zodiac. We then took the pathway of wooden platform steps that brought us to the bird-eye view of the beautiful blue sea and the rocky cliffs containing the awesome columnar joints that are typically at the base of the cliff. The platform only showcases a section of the 2 km stretch of these rocky cliffs. Along the platform, there is a display in English and Korean that educate you about the origin of the rocks. It would be good if another display would be able to pictorially illustrate the geography and formation. According to the information, the columnar joints were formed from the lava flows from the Nokhajiak scoria cone from 140,000 to 250,000 years ago. During cooling of the molten lava, contraction occurred and split the basaltic rocks into polygonal columns. We saw mainly tetragonal (4 sided), pentagonal (5-sided) and hexagonal (6-sided) columns. Because the origin of the columnar joints and rocks is volcanic, these are black. Throughout the time, I stood there simply awestruck by what I saw ? it?s like a divine being had creatively sculptured these columnar joints to perfection. And why only at this 2km stretch and not at other coastal areas in Jeju since the volcanic molten lava flowed everywhere?  It?s a pity the waves that crashed onto the joints and rocks were not huge; otherwise I think it would be an even more awesome sight. There are several pointers to take note:(1) You could appreciate this attraction in less than 1 hour (including photo and selfie-taking)(2) As the attraction is outdoors, be prepared for what the weather will throw at you. Carry an umbrella or wear a cap or sunglasses or put on sunscreen on a sunny day(3) To see these rocks better, I suggest bringing along a pair of binoculars or zooming closer using your camera telephoto lens or your handphone(4) Take plenty of photographs but do not climb over or lean over too much the platform ?railings?We ranked Daepo Jusangjeolli Cliff as one of the top 3 attractions in Jeju. For sure, this Nature?s awesome masterpiece is not to be missed!

My family and I drove to this awesome natural attraction and walked along the layered rocks and cliffs produced as a result of a volcanic eruption on a beautiful non-windy and sunny morning. Safety concerns: Yeongmeori (Dragon's Head) Coast is opened from 8 am to 6:30 pm from May to September. It will be closed when the weather changes in a way that impacts people?s safety (e.g. high tidal waves, strong winds), so it is better to call to check before going. Also a rainy day means that the rocks and coast will become slippery and you may have problems taking photographs. in any case, you definitely need a good pair of walking shoes.2 walking trails: You have to take note that there are 2 trails and entrances to Yeongmeori Coast. Both trails meet each other but are not connected due to safety issue, which means you have to pay separate entrance fees. However, I saw a white bridge is presently being constructed that links the 2 trails, but it remains unclear as to when it will be opened. Between the 2 trails ? Trail 1 and Trail 2 (described below) ? I found Trail 2 to be  safer for walking and has more spectacular sandstone rock formations and cliffs, and because of that my family and I spent about 3 hours admiring the attraction and taking photographs.  Trail 1: This trail is where the tourists go, and starts after the Hamel Castaway Memorial and the Hamel vessel. You park your car (along with the tour coaches) at a car park that?s next to a mini theme park (with the Viking amongst others). You then walk along the seaside promenade next to sandstone layered rocks along the sea, which takes about 1.5 to 3 hours return after the ticket booth (1,000 won for adults & 500 won for teenagers & children). Since certain stretches of the promenade are narrow, you have to walk carefully so as not to fall into the sea and onto the rocks.Trail 2:  This is a shorter trail that in theory should only take about 30-60 minutes return after the ticket booth. You park your car just beneath the temple. Parking is free. Cross the road and look for 3 bronze circular structures with inscriptions of ?Jeju Island Geopark?, ?Global Geopark Networks? and ?New 7 Wonders of Nature? and a green signage ?Yongmeori Coast Entrance -> 300m? From there, you just walk down the steps and follow the path which will take you past several shops. After about 10 minutes? walk, you will reach a ticket booth. After buying the tickets (1,000 won for adults & 500 won for teenagers & children), turn left and you would come to the top of a narrow and steep passageway to the coast. Take your time to carefully choose the big rocks as your steps for your descent (and then I realised what the term ?stepping stone? means). There are no handrails. Once you reached the bottom after about 6 minutes (longer when there are many people), turn around and look up at the challenging and difficult passageway and appreciate your achievement! Looking across the sea, we saw Mount Hallasan. Instead of going left, I recommend you go to the right and once through a archway or hole in a rock wall, and you will soon encounter the spectacular irregular layered and wavy sandstone cliffs that often contain ?pot-holes?. The rock formation at certain places was carved out by  a blade that cut itself into the layered rocks, creating v-shaped clefts. And when the waves crashed into the rocks, it sounds like roaring thunder ? awesome!  There?s a short cement bridge where standing on it allows you to take a superb photograph of the rock formation and the narrow stretch of turquoise-coloured sea. It is also around this same spot that you can take another superb photograph of the cliffs with Mount Sanbangsan in the background. There were 2 ladies (I didn?t think they were the famed ?Haenyeo? sea-divers) at the shoreline with 3 basins of sea animals - sea snail (sora), sea squirt (myeonggye) and sea cucumber (haesam) ? who would be happy to enable you  to experience Korean culture of eating raw seafood by the shoreline. I didn?t like to eat raw seafood so I didn?t try.Overall, my family and I think that Yeongmeori Coast is one attraction in Jeju that ranks it as among the top 3 attractions in Jeju. Don?t miss it! It will blow your mind away!

Love Hallim Park! My expectation was a quick walk around an outdoor park, but it was so much more! Easily taking an entire day if you want it to, you can meander through under ground lava tubes, fruit orchards, small animal zoos, bonsai tree forests, etc.! Highly recommended.

Jeju Hallim Park is a field of frontier spirit of a man who transformed a wasteland to a green paradise. Consisting nine different theme gardens and seasonal festivals, Hallim park is an international tourist attraction of Jeju island, South Korea exhibiting global species of plants and animals. It is 80 acre big and has nearly 1.2 million visitors every year. Visitor can also enjoy Jeju's traditional cuisine in our restaurants. (Gardens) 1. Subtropical botanic garden 2. Palm tree avenue 3. Wild grass and flower garden 4. Hyeopjae and Ssangyong cave 5. Jeju stone and bonsai garden 6. Jae-am folk village 7. Bird garden 8. Jeju stone exhibit hall 9. Water garden (Seasonal Festivals) Jan. - Daffodil Feb. - Ume flower Mar. - Tulip Apr. - Cherry blossoms May - Wild flower Jun. - Hydrangea Jul. thru Sep. - Water lily and lotus Oct. - Pumpkin Nov. - Chrysanthemum Dec. - Camelia (Restaurants and Cafe) - Palm tree restaurant - Dolharubang restaurant - Herb cafe

It's good for photo taking as there are many cute bears all over. There are also good displays , but it is not entirely bears, as there are many other animals there too. The day we visited it, it was very foggy. Oh, and some teddies looked quite  old and worn.Overall, nothing much except photo taking. Hope this review was useful.
It's a showcase of animal dolls. The exhibit was made to look like a zoo with stuffed animals. It was boring for me though, but my daughter like it.

It worth a look just to see the beautiful coastline of the Island.Most of the rocks come in various heights and sizes shaped like hexagons and if you look at certain angles, they can take on various animals etc.The black lava colour offsets against the outstanding sea and coastline.These cliffs are very similar to the Giants Causeway in Ireland with a pancake rock system but on a much smaller scale.It was crowded the day were there and we assume it is the same most days in the summer months. So a lot of people were snaking along this narrow path around the cliffs and we needed to wait our turn to see over the barriers.There are a few stallholders near the carpark (fee charged) selling fruit, souvenirs and the local home made confectionary similar to nougat.On the way out you can go to a park with some gardens and perhaps a museum type building.The hours vary seasonally however it is the standard KRW 2,000 entry fee for most monuments around the Island.Place it on your ?must see? places to visit here just for the dramatic coastline and on a rough day you may get some blow hole situations with the force of the water.Enjoy your visit!
It was a nice mix of gardens, animals, nature (caves).  Good for families.  Not great in anything but a good variety to keep everyone interested.

It is not only a botanical garden. They also have local animals on display, their cave system is quite big with three caves and their bonsai garden is beautiful. You could easily spend here a whole day. 12.000 won per adult sounded pricey at the beginning but these huge gardens and animals need a lot of maintenance and are in good conditions. We enjoyed our visit.

It is a lava tunnel. It's interesting to see but not a must-see. There were some stairs to descent into the tunnel at the entry and it gets pretty dark inside. Your eyes will need to adjust, and there isn't any place to grip along the wall. Please wear comfortable shoes and some layers since it gets wet and chilly inside. Walking paths are uneven on some areas, and most are not well-lit. The tunnel is purposely not well-lit to preserve the natural habitat of its resident animals. A round trip from the entrance will take about 30-40 mins if you're strolling through the tunnel. We visited this cave as part of Yeha East course tour. If you have interest in geological formation, stalagmite, and nature, you may find it interesting.

I'm told that Jeju Island is called   The Hawaii of Asia  . As a Hawaii resident, I'd have to say that Jeju is very similar to Hawaii, and never more so than in Hallim Tropical Park. I felt very much like Hawaii, with lots of lush vegetation, birds, animals and humid weather! If you enjoy nature and the outdoors, you'll enjoy this park!

I went in a hot summer day so I can't judge. It has different plants, animals, folk village and cave. If you interest in these things you might like it. I went there because I have free time to spend but I think if the weather is better it will be different

I was not sure what to expect when we went to Hallim Park, but we really enjoyed it. It's a really nice walk, with flowers, statues waterfalls, caves and animals. It's nice to get away from the city noises if you have been on the mainland for a while. It's not a place you can spend an entire day, and for us was a bit of a trek to get there so make sure you plan your day to only be there a couple of hours.

I was looking forward to this attraction more than any other on Jeju and it didn't disappoint.  I wouldn't rate as #1 (more   touristy   than expected) but worth the stop.  If you can move past the gift stores selling trinkets, cheezy signage, animals in tiny cages and crowds, the attractions within the park are quite beautiful.  I especially liked the lava caves and the bonsai garden.  Those two areas alone were worth the stop.  If you have time, just past the park entrance is a stunning beach area.  Great for photos and possibly a toe dipped into the waters.

i thought the museum sounded stupid but it was actually really cute!!! there were so many scenes set up with stuffed animals on the first floor.  they were so creative!  then you can you to the second floor and take pictures.  there's the rock band set up, the proposal bear, and many more.  there are also famous works of art re-done with teddy bears. finally there's the gift shop.  everything is over priced but you can't expect anything else...

I really enjoy my visit to this site at Jeju island... Recommended for those who loves to take a short hike and enjoy sunrise... The view of the city from the top of it is also beautiful... I literally went gaga after stepping into the museum. You can play with the stuffed animals ergo, take pictures. There are lots of exhibits from safaris to castles. It's very interesting. All the toys are very clean and well-maintained. Kids would definitely enjoy this place.

I am not overly interested in much to with botany but if I were I think I would have enjoyed this park much more. Hallim Park isn't worth making a special journey to go and see. The gardens and varying different areas don't have anything especially interest to see. The animals kept along side the plants are kept in cramped dirty cages and look awful. The tulip garden was pretty, as was were the bonsai trees.

Hallim Park is really a variety of interesting elements of Jeju Island rolled into one. The cave located within Hallim park is one of the main attractions. Other attractions include a multitude of gardens, some animal exhibits, and even a small recreated folk village.If you have more than 3-4 days on Jeju island, I would highly recommend Hallim Park. It can be combined with the excellent Hyopjae Beach located close by. Great day for families. If you are staying less than 3 days, it would probably be best to focus on the main natural attractions Jeju Island is so famous for.I enjoyed exploring the park, taking some pictures with my wife, and then relaxing at the beach.

Hallim Park is quite a beautiful park. There are so many things to see, and the flora is really quite spectacular; however, the living conditions of the animals in the park killed the whole experience for us. The turtles are in aquariums that are much too small, and the aquariums don't contain any kind of natural vegetation for the turtles. In fact, only a few turtles had only a single rock in their containers. If that wasn't depressing enough, the living conditions of the peacocks were, quite simply, inhumane. Although some lucky peacocks got to roam around in an area that was relatively open, most of the peacocks were living in small enclosures and sharing those enclosures with up to 13 other peacocks. There was hardly enough room for them to move around, and the birds seemed to be living in quite stressful conditions.  Then, there were the ostriches. All of the ostriches we saw had a terrible looking skin condition, and most of them were going bald. Compared to the flora in the park, it just seemed like the park put no effort into properly caring for the animals at all. If Hallim Park would put a little more effort into making sure their animals are properly cared for and provide better living conditions for the animals, I would recommend going to this place. However, with the current living conditions of the animals, I absolutely cannot recommend anyone go to this place.

Eat al fresco at the nearby restaurant across from the healing-stone throne is and check out their fresh   ginseng of the sea   (slices of a raw sea-cucumber-like animal). Back in the days of yore --  how far back, no one can be certain --  three demigods came forth from three holes in the ground located near the northern coast of an island to the south of Korea.  These three demigods lived as hunter-gatherers until a ship arrived bearing three princesses, domesticated farm animals and seeds for growing grain. The princesses married with the demigods, and the Tamna Kingdom was born. Today, we know Tamna, which ended in 1404 with the coming of the Joseon Kings -- Korea's last imperial dynasty -- as Jejudo or Jeju Island.  We know that beloved and mystical site as Samseonghyeol (  sam   means three in Korean). It is a special place and, particularly for history buffs, a   must-see   in Jeju.  The holes, which likely were once active thermal vents on this volcanic isle, are surrounded by a protective Stonehenge-like ring and a mini-forest/park of lush and majestic, mature trees and flowers.  It is quite pleasant, and on a warm summer's day, a cool respite from the city that has grown around it.  There's a small museum showing a film about the founding of Tamna.  The film is in Korean, but if you look at the exhibits there before watching the film, you will understand it much better.  It is not readily possible to actually photograph the holes unless you have a ladder, a drone, a long selfie stick or happen to be about 8 feet tall...this would be my one disappointment about the site.  But there is an official photo mounted nearby.  If you have the time, plan to spend 1-1.5 hours there, to take in the walking trails, museum, movie and various historic buildings.  You will also be greeted by some of the original 18th century dolhareubangs (protective   stone grandfathers  ) remaining on the island.  It's a good outing for singles, couples, friends and families.  Even young children can enjoy the birds, flowers, stones and many benches located throughout the park.  Admission is quite nominal...2,500 KRW adults, 1,700 teens; 1,000 children 7-12.

An UNESCO Biosphere Reserve and a World Heritage Site, the Hallasan National Park is loaded with walking trails and is home to South Korea?s highest mountain named the Shield Volcano Hallasan. You?ll find about 1800 different kinds of plants and a number of alpine animals along the way up. The park is a unique place for nature lovers. Settled right in the heart of Jeju island, this park with high density woods and blooming hillsides is concidered as a treat to be at. Transportation: start with chosing a right trail for you. There many different ways up to the mountain, but only one of them will bring you to the summit. To get to the entrance you?d probably need to take one of the public busses or rent a car. Both options are convenient. Equipment: You?d definitely need to be prepared for a long and tiring walk. All the trails are devided into segments, based on their difficulty. Some of the parts of the trail would be paved, some wouldn?t be equipped at all. You?d be grateful for those parts where you?d be able to walk and step on the wooden bridges and paths. But except those short and the easiest parts of the way, you?d need to climb on the steep and narrow rocks, hop along cobblestones and boulders. Timing: don?t rush, remember when you?re on the top, that was only a half of your journey. There is the same long way down the mountain when you?re on the summit. Tips: be prepared for considerable change of the temperature and other weather conditions. We started in a pleasant sunny day and finished when it was drizzling and the fog was literally embracing us. Add up some wind and decreased temperature and you?re almost in our shoes out there. You?d definetely need to wear tracking boots or something alike, protecting and supporting your feet well. Otherwise you  risk hurting your ankles and knees. (as us, cause we were not prepared)You?d also want to change your clothes after 6-7 hours tracking up and down this mountain. Believe me you?ll be sweating af.
